sublevels.description: Security science and technology refer to the interdisciplinary field that combines scientific principles, theories, and technologies to address security challenges and enhance security measures in various domains. It involves the application of scientific methods, engineering, and technological advancements to develop innovative solutions for preventing, detecting, mitigating, and responding to security threats and risks.

sublevels.name: Electronic Devices
sublevels.description: Electronic devices are components for controlling the flow of electrical currents for the purpose of information processing and system control. Prominent examples include transistors and diodes. Electronic devices are usually small and can be grouped together into packages called integrated circuits. This miniaturization is central to the modern electronics boom.

sublevels.name: Electronic Materials
sublevels.description: Electronic materials are materials studied and used mainly for their electrical properties. The electric response of materials largely stems from the dynamics of electrons, and their interplay with atoms and molecules. A material can be classified as a conductor, semiconductor or insulator according to its response to an external electric field.

sublevels.name: Spintronics
sublevels.description: Spintronics is the use of a fundamental property of particles known as spin for information processing. In many ways, spintronics is analogous to electronics, which instead uses the electrical charge on an electron. Carrying information in both the charge and spin of an electron potentially offers devices with a greater diversity of functionality.

sublevels.name: Molecular Electronics
sublevels.description: Molecular electronics is the use of molecules as the primary building block for electronic circuitry. A molecular approach, it is hoped, will enable the construction of much smaller circuits than is currently possible using the more conventional semiconductors such as silicon. The motion of the electrons in such devices is inherently governed by quantum mechanics. + Molecular electronics is the study and application of molecular building blocks for the fabrication of electronic components.

sublevels.name: Measurement Science and Instrumentation
sublevels.description: Measurement Science and Instrumentation covers all aspects of the theory, practice and application of measurement, instrumentation and sensing across science and engineering.

sublevels.name: Metrology
sublevels.description: Nanometrology is a branch of metrology concerned with measurements at the nanoscale. It develops both new measurement techniques and standards. Some of the most common techniques used in nanometrology are atomic force microscopy, electron microscopy and X-ray diffraction.

sublevels.name: Nanometrology
sublevels.description: Nanometrology is a branch of metrology concerned with measurements at the nanoscale. It develops both new measurement techniques and standards. Some of the most common techniques used in nanometrology are atomic force microscopy, electron microscopy and X-ray diffraction.

sublevels.name: Accelerator Physics
sublevels.description: Accelerator Physics concernes with designing, building and operating particle accelerators. It can be described as the study of motion, manipulation and observation of relativistic charged particle beams and their interaction with accelerator structures by electromagnetic fields.

sublevels.name: Medical Physics
sublevels.description: Medical Physics is a branch of Applied Physics, pursued by medical physicists, that uses physics principles, methods and techniques in practice and research for the prevention, diagnosis and treatment of human diseases with a specific goal of improving human health and well-being.

sublevels.name: Radiation Dosimetry and Radiation Protection
sublevels.description: Dosimetry measure, calculates, and assesses the exposure of individuals and the environment to ionizing radiation. It encompasses the development and application of dosimetric techniques to quantify radiation doses received by biological tissues, ensuring that exposure levels remain within safe limits to prevent harmful effects. Radiation protection tires to minimize radiation risks in medical, industrial, and research settings. Key components include the use of dosimeters, which are devices that measure radiation exposure, and the establishment of guidelines and standards for radiation safety, aimed at safeguarding public health and the environment.

sublevels.name: Medical Imaging
sublevels.description: Medical imaging is the technique and process of imaging the interior of a body for clinical analysis and medical intervention, as well as visual representation of the function of some organs or tissues (physiology). Medical imaging seeks to reveal internal structures hidden by the skin and bones, as well as to diagnose and treat disease. Medical imaging also establishes a database of normal anatomy and physiology to make it possible to identify abnormalities.  (Although imaging of removed organs and tissues can be performed for medical reasons, such procedures are usually considered part of pathology instead of medical imaging.)

sublevels.name: Radiography
sublevels.description: Radiography is the use of X-rays or gamma rays to examine non-uniformly composed material; images are recorded on a sensitized surface, such as photographic film or a digital detector. Medical radiography includes examination of any part of the body for diagnostic purposes, such as detecting fractures or a bowel obstruction.

sublevels.name: Tomography
sublevels.description: Tomography is a technique whereby a subject is imaged in 'slices' or sections. Typically the imaging modality is X-ray radiography, and the slices can be viewed separately or in combination. Except for health sciences and medicine the method is also used in other areas of science, such as archaeology, biology, atmospheric science, geophysics, oceanography, plasma physics, materials science and astrophysics.

sublevels.name: Nuclear Medicine
sublevels.description: Nuclear medicine is a specialized area of radiology that uses very small amounts of radioactive materials, or radiopharmaceuticals, to examine organ function and structure. Nuclear medicine imaging is a combination of many different disciplines. These include chemistry, physics, mathematics, computer technology, and medicine. This branch of radiology is often used to help diagnose and treat abnormalities very early in the progression of a disease, such as thyroid cancer.

sublevels.name: Astronomy, Cosmology and Space Sciences
sublevels.description: Astronomy and space science are the study of objects and phenomena that are found inside and beyond our solar system. This combines theoretical work, numerical simulations and observation with both terrestrial and space-craft-borne instruments of the electromagnetic radiation, high-energy particles, and gravitational radiation emitted by astronomical objects.Cosmology deals with the origin, development and structure of the cosmos at large.

sublevels.name: Astrophysics
sublevels.description: Using physics methods or theories to obtain data and understand astronomical objects.

sublevels.name: Particle Astrophysics
sublevels.description: Particle astrophysics, is a branch of particle physics that studies elementary particles of astronomical origin and their relation to astrophysics and cosmology.

sublevels.name: Astrophysical Plasma
sublevels.description: Astrophysical plasma is plasma outside of the solar system. The plasma is made by electrically-charged particles that are susceptible to influences by local electromagnetic fields. E.g. strong fields generated by stars, and weak fields which exist in star forming regions, in interstellar space, and in intergalactic space.

sublevels.name: Nuclear Astrophysics
sublevels.description: Nuclear astrophysics aims to understand the origin of the chemical elements and the energy generation in stars.It is an interdisciplinary branch of physics involving stellar modeling, measurement and theoretical estimation of nuclear reaction rates, physical cosmology and cosmochemistry, gamma ray, optical and X-ray astronomy.

sublevels.name: Dark Energy and Dark Matter
sublevels.description: The dark energy is an unknown form of energy which is hypothesized to permeate all of space, tending to accelerate the expansion of the universe. Two proposed forms for dark energy are the cosmological constant, representing a constant energy density filling space homogeneously, and scalar fields such as quintessence or moduli, dynamic quantities whose energy density can vary in time and space.Dark matter is a hypothetical form of matter that is thought to account for approximately 85% of the matter in the universe, and about a quarter of its total energy density. The majority of dark matter is thought to be non-baryonic in nature, possibly being composed of some as-yet undiscovered subatomic particles.

sublevels.name: Planetary Science
sublevels.description: Planetary science is the study of the celestial bodies that orbit stars, with a particular focus on our own solar system. This includes studying the formation and evolution of planets, the moons and rings that orbit them, and other smaller bodies such as asteroids and comets.

sublevels.name: Astrobiology
sublevels.description: Astrobiology makes use of molecular biology, biophysics, biochemistry, chemistry, astronomy, physical cosmology, exoplanetology and geology to investigate the possibility of life on other worlds and help recognize biospheres that might be different from that on Earth.

sublevels.name: Astronomy, Observations and Techniques
sublevels.description: Study of observing celestial objects with the use of telescopes and other astronomical instruments.

sublevels.name: Space Physics
sublevels.description: Space physics is the study of the natural phenomenon that occur in our solar system. Specifically, the sun, the particles and radiation it creates and how these affect the planets. This includes the solar wind and its interaction with the Earth and near-Earth space; so-called space weather.

sublevels.name: Astrophysical Plasma
sublevels.description: Astrophysical plasma is plasma outside of the solar system. The plasma is made by electrically-charged particles that are susceptible to influences by local electromagnetic fields. E.g. strong fields generated by stars, and weak fields which exist in star forming regions, in interstellar space, and in intergalactic space.

sublevels.name: Astrochemistry
sublevels.description: Astrochemistry is the study of the abundance and reactions of molecules in the Universe, and their interaction with radiation.

sublevels.name: Solar Physics
sublevels.description: Solar physics is the study of the fundamental processes occurring in the sun. Primarily this is related to the dynamics of plasmas and their interplay with the sun’s magnetic fields, and how these processes vary in different regions of the sun, from its core to the surrounding corona.

sublevels.name: Cosmology
sublevels.description: Astronomy concerned with the studies of the origin and evolution of the universe, from the Big Bang to today and on into the future. It is the scientific study of the origin, evolution, and eventual fate of the universe

sublevels.name: Foundations of Physics and Cosmology
sublevels.description: This is the branch of physics which together with cosmology deals with foundational issues such as the nature of space and time, the nature of heat and of energy, the concept of irreversibility and probability, the nature of matter and measurement in quantum theory, renormalization, etc.

sublevels.name: Dark Energy and Dark Matter
sublevels.description: The dark energy is an unknown form of energy which is hypothesized to permeate all of space, tending to accelerate the expansion of the universe. Two proposed forms for dark energy are the cosmological constant, representing a constant energy density filling space homogeneously, and scalar fields such as quintessence or moduli, dynamic quantities whose energy density can vary in time and space.Dark matter is a hypothetical form of matter that is thought to account for approximately 85% of the matter in the universe, and about a quarter of its total energy density. The majority of dark matter is thought to be non-baryonic in nature, possibly being composed of some as-yet undiscovered subatomic particles.

sublevels.name: History of Physics and Astronomy
sublevels.description: The history of physics and astronomy is a rich and fascinating journey that spans thousands of years. The history of physics and astronomy is an ongoing story of scientific inquiry and discovery. It involves the efforts of countless scientists, mathematicians, and researchers who have built upon the knowledge and achievements of those who came before them, continuously pushing the boundaries of our understanding of the universe.

sublevels.name: Space Exploration and Astronautics
sublevels.description: Space exploration is the use of astronomy and space technology to explore outer space. While the exploration of space is carried out mainly by astronomers with telescopes, its physical exploration is conducted both by uncrewed robotic space probes and human spaceflight. Space exploration, like its classical form astronomy, is one of the main sources for space science.

sublevels.name: Astrobiology
sublevels.description: Astrobiology makes use of molecular biology, biophysics, biochemistry, chemistry, astronomy, physical cosmology, exoplanetology and geology to investigate the possibility of life on other worlds and help recognize biospheres that might be different from that on Earth.

sublevels.name: Atomic, Molecular and Chemical Physics
sublevels.description: Atomic and molecular physics it the study of the properties, dynamics and interactions of the basic (but not fundamental) building blocks of matter. A crucial component of this is understanding the behaviour of the electrons that surround the atomic nucleus; these dynamics dominate the way atoms and molecules interact with their environment.

sublevels.name: Ultracold Gases
sublevels.description: Ultracold gases are ensembles of atoms held at a temperature near absolute zero. Such systems enable the creation of exotic phenomena such as Bose–Einstein condensation. Ultracold gases are also useful simulating condensed-matter systems because their tunability opens the door to effects that are otherwise difficult to observe.

sublevels.name: Atomic and Molecular Clusters
sublevels.description: Aggregates of atoms or molecules that are bound together by interatomic or intermolecular forces. These clusters exhibit unique properties that differ from those of individual atoms or molecules due to the interactions between their constituent particles.

sublevels.name: Bio- and Macromolecules
sublevels.description: Macromolecules are very large molecules created by the polymerization of smaller subunits. Clusters are large aggregates of atomic or molecular subunits, which are classified according to the nature of the forces holding them together. For example, there can be van der Waals or metallic clusters.

sublevels.name: Molecular Spectroscopy
sublevels.description: Spectroscopy is a branch of science that concerns the investigation and measurement of spectra produced when matter interacts with or gives off electromagnetic radiation. Molecular spectroscopy is the measurement of interactions between electromagnetic waves and matter.

sublevels.name: Atomic and Molecular Structure and Properties
sublevels.description: Characteristics and behavior of individual atoms and molecules. They involve the arrangement of atoms in a molecule or the arrangement of subatomic particles within an atom, as well as the physical and chemical properties that arise from these structures.

sublevels.name: Quantum Electrodynamics, Relativistic and Many-body Calculations
sublevels.description: In particle physics, quantum electrodynamics (QED) is the relativistic quantum field theory of electrodynamics. In essence, it describes how light and matter interact and is the first theory where full agreement between quantum mechanics and special relativity is achieved. QED mathematically describes all phenomena involving electrically charged particles interacting by means of exchange of photons and represents the quantum counterpart of classical electromagnetism giving a complete account of matter and light interaction.  In technical terms, QED can be described as a perturbation theory of the electromagnetic quantum vacuum. Richard Feynman called it "the jewel of physics" for its extremely accurate predictions of quantities like the anomalous magnetic moment of the electron and the Lamb shift of the energy levels of hydrogen.

sublevels.name: Decay Processes
sublevels.description: Decay processes refer to natural or artificial processes in which a substance or particle undergoes a transformation or disintegration over time. Or natural or spontaneous transformation of particles, atoms, or nuclei into other particles or elements over time.

sublevels.name: Laser-Matter Interaction
sublevels.description: Light is generated from a laser as a result of the following process: electrons in a material move from an excited energy level to a lower-lying energy level and produce photons that contribute to the laser beam. Therefore, fundamental interactions between light and matter are the basis for the analysis of laser operation and the properties of laser light.

sublevels.name: Excited States
sublevels.description: Excited states are those quantum states of an atom or a molecule with more energy than the ground state. The understanding of excited states and their relaxation to lower energy states plays an important role in spectroscopy and also lies at the heart of photochemistry.

sublevels.name: Magnetic Resonance (NMR, EPR)
sublevels.description: Magnetic Resonance occurs magnetic systems that posses both Magnetic moments and angular momentum.  The resonance phenomenon occurs when the natural frequency of a magnetic moment precession is in tune with an external field. Magnetic Resonance occurs in magnetizes nuclear spins, electronic moments, and exotic particles like muons.   Nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy is widely used to determine the structure of organic molecules in solution and study molecular physics, crystals as well as non-crystalline materials. NMR is also routinely used in advanced medical imaging techniques.

sublevels.name: Exotic Atoms
sublevels.description: Exotic atoms and molecules are forms of basic matter in which one subatomic particle is replaced by another with the same charge. For instance, an electron can be replaced with a muon, a pion or an antiproton. Positronium is made by swapping the proton in a hydrogen atom for a positron.

sublevels.name: Matter-Antimatter Interactions
sublevels.description: In modern physics, antimatter is defined as matter that is composed of the antiparticles (or "partners") of the corresponding particles of "ordinary" matter. Theoretically, a particle and its anti-particle (for example, a proton and an antiproton) have the same mass, but opposite electric charge, and other differences in quantum numbers. A collision between any particle and its anti-particle partner leads to their mutual annihilation, giving rise to various proportions of intense photons (gamma rays), neutrinos, and sometimes less-massive particle–antiparticle pairs.

sublevels.name: Low- and Highly-charged Ions
sublevels.description: Highly charged ions (HCI) are ions in very high charge states due to the loss of many or most of their bound electrons by energetic collisions or high-energy photon absorption.

sublevels.name: Metrology and Fundamental Constants
sublevels.description: Metrology is the scientific study of measurement. Metrology is divided into three basic overlapping activities. The first being the definition of units of measurement, second the realisation of these units of measurement in practice, and last traceability, which is linking measurements made in practice to the reference standards. These overlapping activities are used in varying degrees by the three basic sub-fields of Metrology. The sub-fields are scientific or fundamental metrology, which is concerned with the establishment of units of measurement, Applied, technical or industrial metrology, the application of measurement to manufacturing and other processes in society, and Legal metrology, which covers the regulation and statutory requirements for measuring instruments and the methods of measurement.

sublevels.name: Atoms and Molecules in External Fields
sublevels.description: Their behavior and properties when subjected to external influences, such as electric, magnetic, or optical fields. The interaction of atoms and molecules with these external fields can lead to a range of effects, including changes in energy levels, electronic transitions, and alterations in their overall behavior

sublevels.name: Synchrotron Techniques
sublevels.description: Synchrotron techniques refer to a set of advanced experimental methods and analytical tools that utilize synchrotron radiation, which is intense and highly collimated electromagnetic radiation produced by charged particles accelerated in a synchrotron facility. common synchrotron techniques include: X-ray Absorption Spectroscopy (XAS), X-ray Diffraction (XRD), X-ray Fluorescence (XRF), X-ray Microscopy.

sublevels.name: X-Ray Spectroscopy
sublevels.description: X-ray spectroscopy is a general term for several spectroscopic techniques for characterization of materials by using x-ray excitation

sublevels.name: Particle Physics
sublevels.description: Particle physics (also high energy physics) is a branch of physics that studies the nature of the particles that constitute matter and radiation. Particle physics investigates the irreducibly smallest detectable particles and the fundamental interactions necessary to explain their behaviour.

sublevels.name: Theoretical Particle Physics
sublevels.description: Theoretical particle physics attempts to develop the models, theoretical framework, and mathematical tools involved in particle physics to understand current experiments and make predictions for future experiments.

sublevels.name: Experimental Particle Physics
sublevels.description: Experimental Particle Physics refers to the experiments developed to understand the fundamental forces and particles of the universe. It applies to electroweak symmetry breaking, heavy flavor physics, searches for physics beyond the Standard Model, matter/antimatter asymmetry, dark matter, single-photon detection, neutrino properties, dark energy.

sublevels.name: Physics Phenomenology
sublevels.description: Physics Phenomenology is the application of theoretical physics to experimental data by making quantitative predictions based upon known theories. In particle physics, it forms a bridge between the mathematical models of theoretical physics and the results of the high-energy particle experiments.

sublevels.name: Quantum Field Theory
sublevels.description: Quantum Field Theory (QFT) is a theoretical framework that combines classical field theory, special relativity, and quantum mechanics and is used to construct physical models of elementary and subatomic particles (in particle physics) and quasiparticles (in condensed matter physics).

sublevels.name: Particle Astrophysics
sublevels.description: Particle astrophysics, is a branch of particle physics that studies elementary particles of astronomical origin and their relation to astrophysics and cosmology.

sublevels.name: Plasma Physics
sublevels.description: Plasma physics is the study of a state of matter comprising charged particles. Plasmas are usually created by heating a gas until the electrons become detached from their parent atom or molecule.

sublevels.name: Laser-produced Plasma
sublevels.description: Laser-produced plasmas are plasmas produced by firing high-intensity beams of light. Laser-produced plasmas have been used to create short bursts of x-rays and to accelerate particles — so-called plasma-based accelerators. Laser produced plasmas are also useful for recreating astrophysical plasmas in the laboratory.

sublevels.name: Plasma-based Accelerators
sublevels.description: Plasma-based accelerators use plasmas to increase the kinetic energy of charged particles such as electrons, protons, and ions. Plasma-based accelerators usually use laser-produced plasmas in which charge neutrality is broken in a localized area. The plasma-based approach enables devices much smaller than conventional particle accelerators.

sublevels.name: Magnetic and Inertial Plasma Confinement
sublevels.description: Plasma confinement refers to the containment of a plasma by various forces at the extreme conditions necessary for thermonuclear fusion reactions. In the laboratory, researchers use strong magnetic fields to confine plasma. This magnetic confinement strategy may allow them to confine fusion grade plasmas over the long term. Another confinement strategy relies on the inertia of imploding matter. Laboratories use high power lasers or electrical discharges, to compress hydrogen fuel to very high densities for billionths of a second.

sublevels.name: Plasma Processing
sublevels.description: Plasma processing is a plasma-based material processing technology that aims at modifying the chemical and physical properties of a surface. Plasma processing techniques include:plasma activation, plasma ashing, plasma cleaning, plasma electrolytic oxidation, plasma etching, plasma functionalization, plasma polymerization, corona treatment andplasma modification.

sublevels.name: Microplasmas
sublevels.description: Microplasmas are plasmas of small dimensions, ranging from tens to thousands of micrometers. Microplasmas can be generated at a variety of temperatures and pressures, existing as either thermal or non-thermal plasmas. Since that they can be easily sustained and manipulated under standard conditions, they can be employed for commercial, industrial, and medical applications.

sublevels.name: Ultracold Plasmas
sublevels.description: Ultracold plasma is a state of matter where an ionised gaseous becomes increasingly electrically conductive and is cooled down to absolute zero. In these systems the electrostatic interactions between the charges dominate their random thermal motion.

sublevels.name: Plasma Diagnostics
sublevels.description: Plasma diagnostics are a pool of methods, instruments, and experimental techniques used to measure properties of a plasma, such as plasma components' density, distribution function over energy (temperature), their spatial profiles and dynamics, which enable to derive plasma parameters.

sublevels.name: Basic Plasma Phenomena and Gas Discharges
sublevels.description: Plasma and ionized gases have properties and behaviours unlike those of the other states, and the transition between them is mostly a matter of nomenclature and subject to interpretation. Based on the temperature and density of the environment that contains a plasma, partially ionized or fully ionized forms of plasma may be produced.

sublevels.name: Complex Plasma
sublevels.description: Complex plasma (also known as dusty plasma) is a plasma containing millimeter to nanometer sized particles suspended in it. Dusty plasma are interesting because the presence of particles significantly alters the charged particle equilibrium leading to different phenomena.

sublevels.name: Plasma Medicine
sublevels.description: Plasma medicine is an emerging field that combines plasma physics, life sciences and clinical medicine. It is being studied in disinfection, healing, and cancer. Most of the research is in vitro and in animal models.It uses ionized gas for medical uses or dental applications. Plasma, often called the fourth state of matter, is an ionized gas containing positive ions and negative ions or electrons, but is approximately charge neutral on the whole. The plasma sources used for plasma medicine are generally low temperature plasmas, and they generate ions, chemically reactive atoms and molecules, and UV-photons. These plasma-generated active species are useful for several bio-medical applications such as sterilization of implants and surgical instruments as well as modifying biomaterial surface properties.

sublevels.name: Waves, Instabilities and Nonlinear Plasma Dynamics
sublevels.description: Waves, instabilities, and nonlinear plasma dynamics are fundamental phenomena and areas of study in plasma physics. Plasma, often referred to as the fourth state of matter, is a highly ionized gas consisting of charged particles (ions and electrons) that exhibit collective behavior and respond to electromagnetic forces.

sublevels.name: High Temperature Plasma
sublevels.description: High temperature plasma (hot plasma) in one which approaches a state of local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE). A hot plasma is also called a thermal plasma.

sublevels.name: Nuclear Fusion
sublevels.description: Nuclear fusion is a reaction in which two or more atomic nuclei are combined to form one or more different atomic nuclei and subatomic particles (neutrons or protons). The difference in mass between the reactants and products is manifested as either the release or absorption of energy. This difference in mass arises due to the difference in atomic "binding energy" between the atomic nuclei before and after the reaction.

sublevels.name: Atmospheric Pressure Plasmas
sublevels.description: Atmospheric pressure plasma is a plasma in which the pressure approximately matches that of the surrounding atmosphere. For plasma generation various forms of excitation are distinguished: AC excitation, DC and low-frequency excitation, excitation by means of radio waves and microwave excitation.

sublevels.name: Turbulence in Plasmas
sublevels.description: Plasma turbulence is a phenomenon seen in fusion plasmas, and magnetic reconnection, energetic particles and plasma astrophysics. Turbulent processes are the main cause for the particle and energy losses observed. The plasma free energy is released through the excitation of unstable waves or eigenmodes.

sublevels.name: Low Temperature Plasma
sublevels.description: Low temperature plasma is a partially ionized gas containing a variety of ions, electrons, active molecules, electric fields and ultraviolet radiation

sublevels.name: Warm and dense matter
sublevels.description: Warm dense matter can refer to either equilibrium or non-equilibrium states of matter in a (loosely defined) regime of temperature and density between condensed matter and hot plasma. It can be defined as the state that is too dense to be described by weakly coupled plasma physics yet too hot to be described by condensed matter physics. In this state, the potential energy of the interaction between electrons and nuclei and the kinetic energy of electrons are of roughly the same magnitude. The temperature is of the order of the Fermi energy. A commonly occurring type of WDM, created using ultra-fast laser pulses, may exist for a short time in a two-temperature quasi-equilibrium form where the electrons are very hot and have a temperature different from the ions. WDM has a density of the same order of magnitude as a solid (typically somewhere between 0.01 and 100 grams per cc) and a temperature on the order of several thousand kelvins (typically somewhere between 0.5 and 100 electronvolts/Boltzmann constant, in the units favored by practitioners). In effect, WDM is a sub-category of warm-correlated matter.  WDM is expected in the cores of giant planets, brown dwarfs, and small stars. WDM is also created in the inertial confinement fusion context during the solid to plasma phase transition driven by laser pulses, and other systems that start as solids and are heated to become strongly interacting plasmas. The latter two categories imply that WDM physics are also relevant not only to nuclear explosions, but also to atmospheric entry from space, ablation of metals, laser-machining of materials etc. In effect, warm dense matter is also created during intense laser-target interactions[2] and particle beam-target interactions.

sublevels.name: Astrophysical Plasma
sublevels.description: Astrophysical plasma is plasma outside of the solar system. The plasma is made by electrically-charged particles that are susceptible to influences by local electromagnetic fields. E.g. strong fields generated by stars, and weak fields which exist in star forming regions, in interstellar space, and in intergalactic space.

sublevels.name: Nuclear Physics
sublevels.description: Nuclear physics is the field of physics that studies atomic nuclei and their constituents and interactions.

sublevels.name: Superheavy Elements
sublevels.description: Superheavy elements (SHEs) are elements that have an atomic number greater than that of naturally occurring elements. They are extremely heavy, with atomic numbers typically exceeding 104. These elements are highly unstable and usually exist for only a fraction of a second before decaying into lighter elements through radioactive decay

sublevels.name: Experimental Nuclear Physics
sublevels.description: Experimental nuclear physics is the practical investigation of the processes that occur at the heart of an atom. This includes building a better fundamental understanding of fusion and fission, and harnessing them for sustained energy generation.

sublevels.name: Theoretical Nuclear Physics
sublevels.description: Theoretical nuclear physics is a branch of physics that focuses on understanding the properties, behavior, and interactions of atomic nuclei using theoretical and mathematical models. It aims to describe the structure, dynamics, and reactions of atomic nuclei and the fundamental forces that govern them. Theoretical nuclear physicists develop and apply theoretical frameworks, computational methods, and mathematical models to study nuclear phenomena

sublevels.name: Nuclear Fission
sublevels.description: Fission occurs when a neutron slams into a larger atom, forcing it to excite and split into two smaller atoms—also known as fission products. Additional neutrons are also released that can initiate a chain reaction. When each atom splits, a tremendous amount of energy is released.

sublevels.name: Nuclear Astrophysics
sublevels.description: Nuclear astrophysics aims to understand the origin of the chemical elements and the energy generation in stars.It is an interdisciplinary branch of physics involving stellar modeling, measurement and theoretical estimation of nuclear reaction rates, physical cosmology and cosmochemistry, gamma ray, optical and X-ray astronomy.

sublevels.name: Environmental Physics
sublevels.description: Environmental Physics studies the application of principles of physics to problems in the natural environment, including measurements and analyses of interactions between organisms and their environment.

sublevels.name: Philosophical Foundations of Physics and Astronomy
sublevels.description: The philosophical foundations of physics and astronomy involve the exploration of the fundamental principles, concepts, and assumptions that underpin these scientific disciplines. It delves into the philosophical questions and implications raised by our understanding of the physical world and the cosmos.

sublevels.name: Philosophy of Physics
sublevels.description: In philosophy, philosophy of physics deals with conceptual and interpretational issues in modern physics, many of which overlap with research done by certain kinds of theoretical physicists.

sublevels.name: Conceptual Development in Physics
sublevels.description: This category comprises physics concepts and topics. They include common physical phenomena, physical quantities and physics equations (and formula, relations) as well as some general concepts in physics

sublevels.name: History of Physics and Astronomy
sublevels.description: The history of physics and astronomy is a rich and fascinating journey that spans thousands of years. The history of physics and astronomy is an ongoing story of scientific inquiry and discovery. It involves the efforts of countless scientists, mathematicians, and researchers who have built upon the knowledge and achievements of those who came before them, continuously pushing the boundaries of our understanding of the universe.

sublevels.name: Education in Physics
sublevels.description: Physics education refers to the methods currently used to teach physics. Physics Education Research refers to an area of pedagogical research that seeks to improve those methods.

sublevels.name: Biographies of Physicists and Astronomers
sublevels.description: It provide insights into the lives, achievements, and contributions of notable individuals in these fields

sublevels.name: Foundations of Physics and Cosmology
sublevels.description: This is the branch of physics which together with cosmology deals with foundational issues such as the nature of space and time, the nature of heat and of energy, the concept of irreversibility and probability, the nature of matter and measurement in quantum theory, renormalization, etc.

sublevels.name: Gravitational Physics
sublevels.description: Gravitational physics is the study of implications of the general theory of relativity, in which gravitation is a consequence of the curvature of space and time. It involves investigations into the mathematical foundations of the theory, the nature of space and time, and theory's relationship with quantum mechanics.

sublevels.name: Classical and Quantum Gravity
sublevels.description: Classical Gravity refers to the theories of gravity obtained without the process of quantisation, namely the theory of General Relativity, extension of the Newtonian Gravity. Quantum Gravity is the field of theoretical physics that attempts to describe the gravitational field according to the principles of quantum mechanics.

sublevels.name: String Theory
sublevels.description: String theory is a theoretical framework in which the point-like particles of particle physics are replaced by one-dimensional objects called strings. It is a theory of quantum gravity.

sublevels.name: Newtonian Physics
sublevels.description: Newtonian physics, also called Newtonian or classical mechanics, is the description of mechanical events—those that involve forces acting on matter—using the laws of motion and gravitation formulated in the late seventeenth century by English physicist Sir Isaac Newton

sublevels.name: Alternative Relativity
sublevels.description: Alternatives to general relativity are physical theories that attempt to describe the phenomenon of gravitation in competition to Einstein's theory of general relativity. There have been many different attempts at constructing an ideal theory of gravity

sublevels.name: General Relativity
sublevels.description: General relativity describes gravitation in a geometrical framework generalizing special relativity and classical mechanics. This term includes theoretical studies of gravity, experimental studies of gravitational waves and observational studies of gravitational lensing, as well as tests of general relativity and laboratory experiments.

sublevels.name: Earth and Environmental Sciences
sublevels.description: Earth and environmental sciences cover all aspects of Earth and planetary sciences, and broadly encompasses solid Earth processes, surface and atmospheric dynamics, Earth system history, climate and climate change, marine and freshwater systems, and ecology. It also considers the interactions between humans and these systems.

sublevels.name: Environmental Sciences
sublevels.description: Environmental science is the multidisciplinary study of all aspects of the Earth’s physical and biological environments. It encompasses environmental chemistry, soil science, ecology, climatology, vegetation cover, marine and freshwater systems, as well as environmental remediation and preservation, and agriculture and land use.

sublevels.name: Energy Policy, Economics and Management
sublevels.description: Energy policy is the scheme in which the government (or any organization) addresses issues related to energy growth and usage including energy production, distribution, and consumption. Energy economics is a broad scientific subject area which includes topics related to supply and use of energy in societies. Energy management is the proactive and systematic monitoring, control and optimization of an organization's energy consumption to conserve use and decrease energy costs.

sublevels.name: Political Economy of Energy
sublevels.description: Political Economy of Energy studies all aspects of energy in relation to law, customs and government.

sublevels.name: Energy Ethics
sublevels.description: Explores the relationship between energy, ethics, and society.

sublevels.name: Energy Security
sublevels.description: Energy security is the association between national security and the availability of natural resources for energy consumption. Access to afforable energy has become essential to the functioning of modern societies and economies.

sublevels.name: Energy Economics
sublevels.description: Energy economics studies human utilization of energy resources and the consequences of that utilization.

sublevels.name: Renewable Energy
sublevels.description: Renewable energy is energy that comes from sources that are readily replenishable on short-timescales. Examples of these are solar radiation, wind, and biomass.

sublevels.name: Wind Energy
sublevels.description: Wind power or wind energy describes the process by which the wind is used to generate mechanical power or electricity. This mechanical power can be used for specific tasks (such as grinding grain or pumping water) or a generator can convert this mechanical power into electricity.

sublevels.name: Geothermal Energy
sublevels.description: Geothermal energy is thermal energy extracted from the Earth's crust. It combines energy from the formation of the planet and from radioactive decay.

sublevels.name: Mathematical Applications in Environmental Science
sublevels.description: Using a mathematical approach for any issues in the environmental sciences.

sublevels.name: Earth and Environmental Modelling
sublevels.description: Earth and Environmental Modelling refers to the use of mathematical models and simulations to understand and predict natural processes and systems on Earth. These models help analyze environmental changes and make informed decisions for environmental protection and resource management.

sublevels.name: Water
sublevels.description: Hydrology is the study of the cycling of water through different reservoirs on Earth. It also refers to the cycling of liquids such as hydrocarbons on other planets. Hydrology focuses on the distribution of water in the subsurface, surface and atmosphere, the chemistry of that water, and the effects of climate on the water cycle.

sublevels.name: Water Quality and Water Pollution
sublevels.description: Water quality refers to the physical, chemical, and biological characteristics of water, which determine its suitability for various uses, such as drinking, recreational activities, agriculture, and industrial processes. When water has high quality, it is safe for human consumption and supports a healthy aquatic ecosystem. However, water pollution occurs when harmful substances are introduced into water bodies, degrading the water quality and posing risks to human health and the environment.

sublevels.name: Environmental Social Sciences
sublevels.description: Environmental social science is the application of social science – broadly the study of the relationship between individuals in their context within society – and its application to our understanding of environmental issues.

sublevels.name: Environmental Economics
sublevels.description: Environmental economics is the study of the economics of ecological and environmental issues. It focuses on the monetary value of ecosystems and the costs and benefits of environmental policies.

sublevels.name: Environmental Policy
sublevels.description: Studies the commitment of an organization or government to the laws, regulations, and other policy mechanisms concerning environmental issues.

sublevels.name: Climate Change Ecology
sublevels.description: Climate-change ecology is the study of the effects of anthropogenic climate change on any aspect of ecology. It includes the effects of altered temperature and precipitation on the distribution, abundance, behaviour and physiology of populations and communities.

sublevels.name: Environmental Law
sublevels.description: Environmental law refers to a system of legal principles, regulations, and statutes that aim to protect and manage the natural environment and address environmental issues. It encompasses a wide range of legal frameworks at international, national, regional, and local levels, governing various aspects of environmental protection, conservation, and sustainable development. Environmental law encompasses both public and private law and involves the interaction between legal, social, economic, and scientific considerations.

sublevels.name: International Environmental Law
sublevels.description: International environmental law is the set of agreements and principles that reflect the world's collective effort to manage our transition to the Anthropocene by resolving our most serious environmental problems, including climate change, ozone depletion and mass extinction of wildlife.

sublevels.name: Climate-Change Policy
sublevels.description: Climate-change policy encompasses policies formulated specifically to tackle climate change and can be local, national or international in scope. These broadly fall into two categories; those designed to minimise the extent of climate change – climate change mitigation – and those intended to minimise risks and seize upon new opportunities – climate change adaptation.

sublevels.name: Climate Change Mitigation
sublevels.description: Climate-change mitigation encompasses policies and activities intended to reduce the greenhouse gas forcing of the climate system. Key intervention points include: the reduction of greenhouse gas sources, for example by reducing deforestation; emissions, for instance low carbon energy generation; and enhancing greenhouse gas sinks, for example by changes in land use.

sublevels.name: Climate Engineering
sublevels.description: Climate Engineering (also called Geoengineering) involves deliberate and purposeful interventions with the aim of mitigating anthropogenic effects on the earth systems. It includes a wide array of technologies centered around, e.g. reflecting sunlight back into space (solar radiation management) or removing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.

sublevels.name: Environmental Chemistry
sublevels.description: Environmental chemistry is the study of chemical processes that occur in water, air, terrestrial and living environments, and the effects of human activity on them. It includes topics such as astrochemistry, atmospheric chemistry, environmental modelling, geochemistry, marine chemistry and pollution remediation. - Chemical ecology is the study integrating chemistry and biology to examine the chemical interactions among organisms and their environment. It includes signalling processes and communication between individuals, for instance in hormone responses.

sublevels.name: Geochemistry
sublevels.description: Geochemistry is the study of the chemical composition of the Earth and other planets, and the chemical processes that affect them.

sublevels.name: Biogeochemistry
sublevels.description: Biogeochemistry is the study of how chemical elements flow through living systems and their physical environments. It investigates the factors that influence cycles of key elements such as carbon, nitrogen and phosphorous.

sublevels.name: Ecotoxicology
sublevels.description: Ecotoxicology is an interdisciplinary field that draws from knowledge and techniques in the fields of ecology and toxicology to study the effects of toxic chemical or biological agents on biological organisms at the population, community or ecosystem level.

sublevels.name: Environmental Management
sublevels.description: Environmental Management focuses on the management of the interaction of societies with the environment, and on their impact on the environment.

sublevels.name: Environmental Biotechnology
sublevels.description: Environmental biotechnology is the branch of biotechnology that addresses environmental problems, such as the removal of pollution, renewable energy generation or biomass production, by exploiting biological processes.

sublevels.name: Environmental Health
sublevels.description: Environmental health studies public health concerned with all aspects of the natural and built environment affecting human health.

sublevels.name: Radiation Dosimetry and Radiation Protection
sublevels.description: Dosimetry measure, calculates, and assesses the exposure of individuals and the environment to ionizing radiation. It encompasses the development and application of dosimetric techniques to quantify radiation doses received by biological tissues, ensuring that exposure levels remain within safe limits to prevent harmful effects. Radiation protection tires to minimize radiation risks in medical, industrial, and research settings. Key components include the use of dosimeters, which are devices that measure radiation exposure, and the establishment of guidelines and standards for radiation safety, aimed at safeguarding public health and the environment.

sublevels.name: Pollution
sublevels.description: Pollution is the introduction of harmful materials into the environment (air, water, soil). It can be naturally caused, e.g. through volcanic ash. Pollution can also be created by human activity, such as trash or runoff produced by factories.

sublevels.name: Water Quality and Water Pollution
sublevels.description: Water quality refers to the physical, chemical, and biological characteristics of water, which determine its suitability for various uses, such as drinking, recreational activities, agriculture, and industrial processes. When water has high quality, it is safe for human consumption and supports a healthy aquatic ecosystem. However, water pollution occurs when harmful substances are introduced into water bodies, degrading the water quality and posing risks to human health and the environment.

sublevels.name: Noise Control
sublevels.description: Noise control studies strategies to reduce noise pollution or to reduce the impact of that noise outdoors and indoors.

sublevels.name: Soil Science
sublevels.description: Study of soil as a natural resource on the surface of the Earth including soil formation, classification and mapping; physical, chemical, biological, and fertility properties of soils; and these properties in relation to the use and management of soils

sublevels.name: Environmental Monitoring
sublevels.description: Environmental monitoring or analysis describes the processes and activities (e.g. sampling and analyzing soil or water, or using analytical chemistry) that need to take place to characterize and monitor the quality of the environment.

sublevels.name: Waste Management and Waste Technology
sublevels.description: Studies on waste management explore activities required to manage waste from its inception to its final disposal. Waste management includes the collection, transport, treatment and disposal of waste, together with monitoring and regulation of the waste management process. Waste (treatment) technology cover landfills, composting, recycling etc.

sublevels.name: Philosophy of Nature
sublevels.description: Explores the universe seeking to understand it from a philospopihcal point of view, linking to environmental ethics.

sublevels.name: Sustainability
sublevels.description: Sustainability is essentially the ability to endure, for example by exploiting resources in a way that does not deplete their future availability or unduly damage the wider environment. This concept has been incorporated in the idea of sustainable development.

sublevels.name: Earth Sciences
sublevels.description: Earth sciences include all fields of natural science related to the planet Earth. It covers the main areas of geology, mineralogy and petrology, geochemistry, geophysics, hydrogeology, oceanography, and atmospheric sciences. It also includes interdisciplinary sciences (earth system sciences) that deal with the interplay of the different earth spheres; lithosphere, hydrosphere, biosphere, cryosphere, and atmosphere.

sublevels.name: Ocean Sciences
sublevels.description: Ocean sciences span the physics, chemistry, and biology of marine systems. The field encompasses ocean circulation, energy dissipation, marine biology, ecology, biogeochemical cycles, water mass formation and movement, ocean temperature and salinity, and marine carbon and carbonate chemistry.

sublevels.name: Biooceanography
sublevels.description: Biooceanography is the study of marine organisms and their interactions with their environment. It includes the ecology and biogeochemistry of marine plants, animals and microbes.

sublevels.name: Climate Sciences
sublevels.description: Climate science is the study of relatively long-term weather conditions, typically spanning decades to centuries but extending to geological timescales. The discipline is primarily concerned with atmospheric properties – for example temperature and humidity – and patterns of circulation, as well as interactions with the ocean, the biosphere, and, over longer timescales, the geosphere.

sublevels.name: Climate Change
sublevels.description: Climate change refers to a statistically defined change in the average and/or variability of the climate system, this includes the atmosphere, the water cycle, the land surface, ice and the living components of Earth. The definition does not usually require the causes of change to be attributed, for example to human activity, but there are exceptions.

sublevels.name: Climate-Change Policy
sublevels.description: Climate-change policy encompasses policies formulated specifically to tackle climate change and can be local, national or international in scope. These broadly fall into two categories; those designed to minimise the extent of climate change – climate change mitigation – and those intended to minimise risks and seize upon new opportunities – climate change adaptation.

sublevels.name: Climate Change Mitigation
sublevels.description: Climate-change mitigation encompasses policies and activities intended to reduce the greenhouse gas forcing of the climate system. Key intervention points include: the reduction of greenhouse gas sources, for example by reducing deforestation; emissions, for instance low carbon energy generation; and enhancing greenhouse gas sinks, for example by changes in land use.

sublevels.name: Climate Engineering
sublevels.description: Climate Engineering (also called Geoengineering) involves deliberate and purposeful interventions with the aim of mitigating anthropogenic effects on the earth systems. It includes a wide array of technologies centered around, e.g. reflecting sunlight back into space (solar radiation management) or removing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.

sublevels.name: Atmospheric Science
sublevels.description: Atmospheric science is the study of the dynamics and chemistry of the layers of gas that surround the Earth, other planets and moons. This encompasses the interactions between various parts of the atmosphere as well as interactions with the oceans and freshwater systems, the biosphere and human activities.

sublevels.name: Meteorology
sublevels.description: Meteorology is the scientific study of the atmosphere that focuses on weather processes and forecasting.

sublevels.name: Earth System Sciences
sublevels.description: Earth System Sciences embrace chemistry, physics, biology, mathematics and applied sciences in transcending disciplinary boundaries to treat the Earth as an integrated system.

sublevels.name: Coastal Sciences
sublevels.description: Coastal Science is an interdisciplinary approach that includes geomorphology, ecology, engineering, technology, oceanography, and human activities as they relate to coasts.

sublevels.name: Biogeosciences
sublevels.description: An interdisciplinary field of study integrating geoscience and biological sciences.

sublevels.name: Microbial Ecology
sublevels.description: Microbial ecology is the study of the interactions of microorganisms with their environment, each other, and plant and animal species. It includes the study of symbioses, biogeochemical cycles and the interaction of microbes with anthropogenic effects such as pollution and climate change.

sublevels.name: Community and Population Ecology
sublevels.description: Community ecology is the study of communities formed of populations of different species. It includes the study of the interactions between species, such as mutualism, predation and competition, and the dynamics and structure of the community.

sublevels.name: Freshwater and Marine Ecology
sublevels.description: Biolimnology or freshwater ecology is the study of all aspects of the ecology of terrestrial aquatic systems, including rivers, lakes and ponds. It includes the community ecology of these ecosystems, as well as ecosystem processes, interactions with adjacent terrestrial and marine ecosystems, and conservation and restoration..Freshwater ecology is the study of all aspects of the ecology of terrestrial aquatic systems, including rivers, lakes and ponds. It includes the community ecology of these ecosystems, as well as ecosystem processes, interactions with adjacent terrestrial and marine ecosystems, and conservation and restoration.

sublevels.name: Molecular Ecology
sublevels.description: Molecular ecology is the use of molecular genetic tools to study ecological questions. Techniques such as microarrays and DNA markers are used to study the interactions and diversity of natural populations.

sublevels.name: Plant Ecology
sublevels.description: Plant Ecology is the branch of ecology that focuses on the relationships between plants and their environment, including interactions with other organisms, climate, soil, and physical factors. It examines how plant species adapt to their habitats, the distribution and abundance of plant communities, and the dynamics of ecosystems. Key areas of study within plant ecology include plant physiology, population dynamics, community structure, and the impact of environmental changes on plant life. This field is essential for understanding biodiversity, ecosystem services, and the effects of human activities on natural habitats.

sublevels.name: Agroecology
sublevels.description: Agroecology is the study of the ecology of terrestrial agricultural systems. It includes both the effects of agricultural practices such as pesticide use on non-domesticated species, and the effect of the ecological environment on crop and livestock yields.

sublevels.name: Biodiversity
sublevels.description: Biodiversity is the variation in living forms and can be measured in ways that include the number of species, functional variety of species, evenness of species distribution or genetic diversity. Biodiversity science investigates levels of biodiversity, its functional effects, and how and why it changes over time.

sublevels.name: Paleoecology
sublevels.description: Palaeoecology is the study of past ecosystems using palaeontological methods. Fossil data are used to reconstruct interactions between different species and between species and their environment.

sublevels.name: Boreal Ecology
sublevels.description: Boreal ecology is the study of ecosystems in the subarctic (boreal) zone of the Northern hemisphere. These areas are dominated by coniferous forest, generally have permafrost soils, and occur below the Arctic tundra latitudes.

sublevels.name: Ecosystems
sublevels.description: Ecosystem ecology is the combined study of the physical and biological components of ecosystems. It focuses on how matter and energy flow through both organisms and the abiotic components of the environment.

sublevels.name: Forestry
sublevels.description: Forestry is the study and practice of the cultivation and management of woodlands. Forests provide goods and services such as timber, recreation and carbon sequestration.

sublevels.name: Wood Science and Technology
sublevels.description: The study of the science and technology of wood and other lignocellulosic materials.

sublevels.name: Conservation Biology
sublevels.description: Conservation biology or Conservation Ecology is a mission-oriented science that focuses on how to protect and restore biodiversity, or the diversity of life on Earth. Like medical research, conservation biology deals with issues where quick action is critical and the consequences of failure are great. To preserve biodiversity, scientists must answer three general questions. First, how is the diversity of life distributed around the planet? Second, what threats does this diversity face? Third, what can people do to reduce or eliminate these threats and, when possible, restore biological diversity and ecosystem health?

sublevels.name: Environmental Law
sublevels.description: Environmental law refers to a system of legal principles, regulations, and statutes that aim to protect and manage the natural environment and address environmental issues. It encompasses a wide range of legal frameworks at international, national, regional, and local levels, governing various aspects of environmental protection, conservation, and sustainable development. Environmental law encompasses both public and private law and involves the interaction between legal, social, economic, and scientific considerations.

sublevels.name: International Environmental Law
sublevels.description: International environmental law is the set of agreements and principles that reflect the world's collective effort to manage our transition to the Anthropocene by resolving our most serious environmental problems, including climate change, ozone depletion and mass extinction of wildlife.

sublevels.name: Terrestrial Ecology
sublevels.description: Terrestrial ecology is the study of how land-based organisms interact with each other and their environment.

sublevels.name: Macroecology
sublevels.description: Macroecology is the study of broad scale ecological patterns and processes. The focus is rarely on single communities and ecosystems, and instead looks at principles that apply more broadly such as metabolic scaling, extinction risk and diversity gradients.

sublevels.name: Theoretical and Statistical Ecology
sublevels.description: Theoretical ecology is the scientific discipline devoted to the study of ecological systems using theoretical methods such as simple conceptual models, mathematical models, computational simulations, and advanced data analysis. Statistical ecology deals with the development of new methodologies for analyzing ecological data.

sublevels.name: Restoration Ecology
sublevels.description: Restoration ecology is the scientific study supporting the practice of ecological restoration, which is the practice of renewing and restoring degraded, damaged, or destroyed ecosystems and habitats in the environment by active human intervention and action.

sublevels.name: Biogeochemistry
sublevels.description: Biogeochemistry is the study of how chemical elements flow through living systems and their physical environments. It investigates the factors that influence cycles of key elements such as carbon, nitrogen and phosphorous.

sublevels.name: Landscape Ecology
sublevels.description: Landscape ecology is the study of the pattern and interaction between ecosystems within a region of interest, and the way the interactions affect ecological processes, especially the unique effects of spatial heterogeneity on these interactions.

sublevels.name: Geotechnical Engineering
sublevels.description: Geotechnical engineering is an area of civil engineering that focuses on the engineering behaviour of earth materials. Using the principles of soil and rock mechanics, it applies knowledge from geology, geophysics, hydrology, and related fields. Typical projects include embankments, tunnels, levees, wharves, landfills, and other structures that are built in or supported by soil and rock.

sublevels.name: Soil and Rock Mechanics
sublevels.description: The subject soil and rock mechanics is the theoretical and applied science of the mechanical behavior of soils and rocks and their application.

sublevels.name: Hydraulic Engineering
sublevels.description: Concerned with the flow and conveyance of fluids, principally water and sewage. Includes the design of bridges, dams, channels, canals, and levees.

sublevels.name: Mining and Exploration
sublevels.description: Mining and exploration are two distinct yet interconnected processes involved in the extraction and discovery of mineral resources from the Earth's crust.

sublevels.name: Underground Engineering and Tunnel Construction
sublevels.description: Underground construction refers to the construction of underground tunnels, shafts, chambers, and passageways, it is also sometimes used to describe the portion of traditional construction that takes place below grade. The method of tunnel construction depends on such factors as the ground conditions, the ground water conditions, the length and diameter of the tunnel drive, the depth of the tunnel, the logistics of supporting the tunnel excavation, the final use and shape of the tunnel and appropriate risk management. Tunnel construction is a subset of underground construction. Underground construction and tunnel engineering is truly an interdisciplinary practice, involving knowledge and skills primarily in civil engineering, geological engineering and mining engineering and, to a lesser extent, mechanical engineering, electrical engineering, geophysics, geology and others.

sublevels.name: Foundation Engineering
sublevels.description: Application of soil mechanics and rock mechanics  in the design of foundation elements of structures.

sublevels.name: Climate Engineering
sublevels.description: Climate Engineering (also called Geoengineering) involves deliberate and purposeful interventions with the aim of mitigating anthropogenic effects on the earth systems. It includes a wide array of technologies centered around, e.g. reflecting sunlight back into space (solar radiation management) or removing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.

sublevels.name: Natural Hazards
sublevels.description: Natural hazards are naturally occurring events that have a negative impact on people or the environment.

sublevels.name: Planetary Science
sublevels.description: Planetary science is the study of the celestial bodies that orbit stars, with a particular focus on our own solar system. This includes studying the formation and evolution of planets, the moons and rings that orbit them, and other smaller bodies such as asteroids and comets.

sublevels.name: Astrobiology
sublevels.description: Astrobiology makes use of molecular biology, biophysics, biochemistry, chemistry, astronomy, physical cosmology, exoplanetology and geology to investigate the possibility of life on other worlds and help recognize biospheres that might be different from that on Earth.

sublevels.name: Geology
sublevels.description: Geology is broadly the study of the Earth and other planets, moons, and smaller planetary bodies. Fields of geology range from the initial formation and differentiation of the Earth to modern surface processes, such as erosion and soil formation, and include Earth system history and the evolution of life.

sublevels.name: Stratigraphy
sublevels.description: Stratigraphy is the study of stratified rocks.

sublevels.name: Geodynamics
sublevels.description: Geodynamics refers to the processes by which mantle convection shapes and reshapes the Earth and other rocky planets. Its study includes plate tectonics, volcanism, the chemistry of lava and volcanic rocks, gravity and geomagnetic anomalies as well as seismic investigations into the structure of the mantle.

sublevels.name: Sedimentology
sublevels.description: Sedimentology is the study of sand, silt, and clay, and the processes that result in their formation (erosion and weathering), transport, deposition and diagenesis. Sedimentary rocks can be, e.g., clastic rocks (sandstone, siltstone,...), carbonate rocks (limestone, dolomite), or evaporites.

sublevels.name: Geophysics
sublevels.description: Geophysics is broadly the study of the physics of planetary bodies and atmospheres, including the flow of energy through these systems. The term may also be used more narrowly to describe the investigation and characterization of the Earth’s subsurface using non-invasive techniques such as seismic imaging.

sublevels.name: Geodesy
sublevels.description: Geodesy is the study of accurately measuring and understanding Earth's geometric shape, orientation in space and gravitational field. The field also incorporates studies of how these properties change over time and equivalent measurements for other planets.

sublevels.name: Mineralogy
sublevels.description: Mineralogy is the study of minerals, the building blocks of rocks, which are naturally-occurring, crystalline solids with a set chemical make-up. This includes the study of the chemical composition and physical properties of minerals, as well as mineral formation and geographic distribution, with particular emphasis on minerals with economic value.

sublevels.name: Paleontology
sublevels.description: Palaeontology is the study of prehistoric species, mostly ones that are extinct. It focuses primarily on fossil data, using a variety of physical, chemical and biological techniques to analyse them.

sublevels.name: Petrology
sublevels.description: Petrology is the study of the macroscopic and microscopic mineralogical and chemical composition of rocks. In addition to assessing sedimentary, igneous, and metamorphic rocks that are accessible at the surface, experimental petrology aims to create high pressure and temperature conditions to investigate what rock types may exist in the Earth’s subsurface.

sublevels.name: Atmospheric Science
sublevels.description: Atmospheric science is the study of the dynamics and chemistry of the layers of gas that surround the Earth, other planets and moons. This encompasses the interactions between various parts of the atmosphere as well as interactions with the oceans and freshwater systems, the biosphere and human activities.

sublevels.name: Meteorology
sublevels.description: Meteorology is the scientific study of the atmosphere that focuses on weather processes and forecasting.

sublevels.name: Geochemistry
sublevels.description: Geochemistry is the study of the chemical composition of the Earth and other planets, and the chemical processes that affect them.

sublevels.name: Biogeochemistry
sublevels.description: Biogeochemistry is the study of how chemical elements flow through living systems and their physical environments. It investigates the factors that influence cycles of key elements such as carbon, nitrogen and phosphorous.

sublevels.name: Geomorphology
sublevels.description: Geomorphology is the study of landforms and landscapes on Earth and other planets, and the processes that shape them. This discipline is primarily concerned with the erosion and deposition of rock and sediments by wind and water, but also includes the creation of topography through tectonics.

sublevels.name: Earth and Environmental Modelling
sublevels.description: Earth and Environmental Modelling refers to the use of mathematical models and simulations to understand and predict natural processes and systems on Earth. These models help analyze environmental changes and make informed decisions for environmental protection and resource management.

sublevels.name: Geography
sublevels.description: Geography is a branch of academic study broadly concerned with the Earth. Geographers can be roughly divided into those concerned with physical earth processes (physical geography), such as erosion and sedimentation, and those who are more concerned with human activities (human geography).

sublevels.name: Human Geography
sublevels.description: Human geography or anthropogeography is the branch of geography that deals with humans and their communities, cultures, economies, and interactions with the environment by studying their relations with and across locations. It analyzes patterns of human social interaction, their interactions with the environment, and their spatial interdependencies by application of qualitative and quantitative research methods.

sublevels.name: Economic Geography
sublevels.description: Economic geography is the subfield of human geography which studies economic activity and factors affecting them. It can also be considered a subfield or method in economics.[1] There are four branches of economic geography.

sublevels.name: Social and Cultural Geography
sublevels.description: Studies the cultural landscapes which are determined by societies developing out of their local landscapes, and those landscaped being shaped on the the other hand by the societies located there. Social/Cultural geography is a complex research field that encloses a variety of subfields such as political and gender studies, anthropology, and sociology.

sublevels.name: Urban Geography
sublevels.description: incl. megacities, cities, towns

sublevels.name: Urban Economics
sublevels.description: Urban Economics studies the economic functions and development of cities, focusing on issues such as land use, housing, transportation, and urban policy.

sublevels.name: Urban Planning
sublevels.description: Urban planning is the process of guiding and directing the use and development of land, urban environment, infrastructure, and related communities to maximise social and environmental outcomes.

sublevels.name: Development Geography
sublevels.description: Studies processes that help to develop local communities; it is a very much practice-orientated or applied discipline, based on sustainable development, economics, equality, social justice, resilience, and the work of social insitutions.

sublevels.name: Social Work and Community Development
sublevels.description: Studies processes that help to develop local communities; it is a very much practice-orientated or applied discipline, based on sustainable development, economics, equality, social justice, resilience, and the work of social insitutions.

sublevels.name: Integrated Geography
sublevels.description: Integrated Geography links human and physical geography; it describes and explains the spatial aspects of interactions between human individuals or societies and their natural environment.

sublevels.name: Economic Geography
sublevels.description: Economic geography is the subfield of human geography which studies economic activity and factors affecting them. It can also be considered a subfield or method in economics.[1] There are four branches of economic geography.

sublevels.name: Environmental Economics
sublevels.description: Environmental economics is the study of the economics of ecological and environmental issues. It focuses on the monetary value of ecosystems and the costs and benefits of environmental policies.

sublevels.name: Physical Geography
sublevels.description: Physical geography is the branch of natural science which deals with the study of processes and patterns in the natural environment such as the atmosphere, hydrosphere, biosphere, and geosphere.

sublevels.name: Geodesy
sublevels.description: Geodesy is the study of accurately measuring and understanding Earth's geometric shape, orientation in space and gravitational field. The field also incorporates studies of how these properties change over time and equivalent measurements for other planets.

sublevels.name: Geomorphology
sublevels.description: Geomorphology is the study of landforms and landscapes on Earth and other planets, and the processes that shape them. This discipline is primarily concerned with the erosion and deposition of rock and sediments by wind and water, but also includes the creation of topography through tectonics.

sublevels.name: Geographical Information System
sublevels.description: A Geographic Information System (GIS) is a system designed to capture, store, manipulate, analyze, manage, and present spatial or geographic data. GIS applications are tools that allow users to create interactive queries (user-created searches), analyze spatial information, edit data in maps, and present the results of all these operations.

sublevels.name: Remote Sensing and Photogrammetry
sublevels.description: Remote sensing collects data in the form of light and color. By detecting different wavelengths of light radiation, it can generate maps. Instead of measuring wavelengths of radiation, on the other hand, photogrammetry uses imagery to measure coordinates in space. Photogrammetry is the science and technology of obtaining reliable information about physical objects and the environment through the process of recording, measuring and interpreting photographic images and patterns of electromagnetic radiant imagery and other phenomena.

sublevels.name: Cartography
sublevels.description: Cartography is the study and practice of making maps. It combines science, aesthtetics and technique in order to model reality and to commicate spatial information effectively.

sublevels.name: Regional Geography
sublevels.description: Geographical studies that specifically cover a certain region of the world.

sublevels.name: Urban Geography
sublevels.description: incl. megacities, cities, towns

sublevels.name: Urban Economics
sublevels.description: Urban Economics studies the economic functions and development of cities, focusing on issues such as land use, housing, transportation, and urban policy.

sublevels.name: Urban Planning
sublevels.description: Urban planning is the process of guiding and directing the use and development of land, urban environment, infrastructure, and related communities to maximise social and environmental outcomes.

data.name: Life Sciences
data.description: Life sciences encompass a broad field of scientific study that focuses on living organisms, including plants, animals, and humans. It involves the exploration and understanding of various aspects of life, ranging from the structure and function of cells and organisms to their interactions within ecosystems.

sublevels.name: Biological Sciences
sublevels.description: Biological sciences encompasses all the divisions of natural sciences examining various aspects of vital processes. The concept includes anatomy, physiology, cell biology, biochemistry and biophysics, and covers all organisms from microorganisms, animals to plants.

sublevels.name: Agriculture
sublevels.description: Agriculture is the cultivation of plants, animals, and some other organisms, such as fungi, for the production of food, fibre, fuel, and medicines used by society. Agricultural science is a broad multidisciplinary field of biology that encompasses the parts of exact, natural, economic and social sciences that are used in the practice and understanding of agriculture.
