sublevels.description: Coaching in the field of psychology is a collaborative and goal-oriented approach to helping individuals achieve personal and professional growth, positive change, and improved well-being. It involves working with a trained coach who uses evidence-based techniques and principles from psychology to help clients identify their strengths, values, and goals, and develop strategies to overcome obstacles and achieve their desired outcomes.

sublevels.name: Team Coaching
sublevels.description: Team coaching and management is a field within human resource management that focuses on improving team performance through coaching and training interventions. It involves using coaching techniques to identify and develop team members' strengths and areas for improvement, as well as improving communication and collaboration within the team.  Topics within team coaching and management may include:  Team building Group dynamics Conflict resolution Communication skills Leadership development Performance management Organizational culture Change management Research in this field may explore the impact of team coaching and management on team performance, as well as the effectiveness of different coaching techniques and interventions. It may also examine the role of team coaching and management in promoting employee engagement, retention, and job satisfaction.

sublevels.name: Consulting
sublevels.description: Consulting in the field of organizational psychology refers to a collaborative and systematic process through which an external consultant, or a team of consultants, works with an organization to identify, diagnose, and solve problems related to human behavior, productivity, and organizational effectiveness. The consultant uses specialized knowledge and skills in psychology, as well as other disciplines, to analyze and interpret data, and provide insights and recommendations to the client organization. The consulting process may involve a range of activities, such as organizational diagnosis, needs assessment, intervention design, implementation planning, and evaluation. The ultimate goal of organizational consulting is to help organizations improve their performance, meet their strategic objectives, and promote the well-being of their employees, stakeholders, and communities.

sublevels.name: Career Counseling
sublevels.description: Career counseling is a specialized subfield of study within psychology that focuses on helping individuals with their career development and decision-making processes. It aims to assist individuals in understanding their interests, skills, values, and personality traits and how they relate to different career options.

sublevels.name: Counseling
sublevels.description: Counseling in the field of psychology refers to a collaborative and therapeutic process through which a trained counselor helps an individual or a group to explore, understand, and manage psychological, emotional, behavioral, or interpersonal issues that may be causing distress or impairing their functioning. The counseling process may involve a range of activities, such as assessment, psychoeducation, counseling sessions, and referrals to other professionals or resources.

sublevels.name: Supervision
sublevels.description: The supervision process may involve a range of activities, such as case consultation, review of clinical work, feedback on performance, and professional development planning. The supervisor uses specialized knowledge and skills in psychology, as well as other disciplines, to facilitate the supervisee's self-reflection, learning, and growth, and to help them address challenges and issues related to their clinical work, research, teaching, or other professional roles. The ultimate goal of supervision is to promote the quality of psychological services, protect the welfare of clients and stakeholders, and support the professional identity and wellbeing of the supervisee.

sublevels.name: Developmental Psychology
sublevels.description: Developmental psychology is a branch of psychology that focuses on understanding how individuals grow, change, and develop across the lifespan. It seeks to study and explain the physical, cognitive, emotional, and social changes that occur from infancy through old age. Developmental psychologists explore various aspects of human development, including motor skills, language acquisition, cognitive abilities, social interactions, emotional development, and the formation of identity. They examine both the typical patterns of development and the individual differences that exist among individuals.

sublevels.name: Personal Development
sublevels.description: Personal development focuses on enhancing one's self-awareness, knowledge, skills, and attitudes with the goal of achieving personal fulfillment and reaching one's potential. It involves a conscious effort to develop and refine aspects of oneself, such as emotional intelligence, self-esteem, resilience, goal-setting, and self-motivation.

sublevels.name: Emotional Development
sublevels.description: Emotional development, in the field of psychology, refers to the gradual acquisition and refinement of emotional skills, understanding, and regulation throughout the lifespan. It involves the development of emotional awareness, expression, and management, as well as the ability to recognize and understand the emotions of oneself and others. Emotional development encompasses various aspects, including the experience and expression of emotions, the understanding of emotional cues and social context, and the regulation of emotions in adaptive and healthy ways. This process is influenced by a combination of genetic, biological, cognitive, and environmental factors, and it plays a vital role in shaping individuals' emotional well-being, social relationships, and overall psychological functioning.

sublevels.name: Physical Development
sublevels.description: Physical development, in the field of psychology, refers to the biological and physiological changes that occur in an individual's body and physical abilities over time. It encompasses various aspects, including changes in body size and proportion, motor skills, sensory abilities, and overall physical health. Physical development starts during prenatal development and continues throughout infancy, childhood, adolescence, and into adulthood. It is influenced by a combination of genetic factors, environmental influences, nutrition, physical activity, and overall health status. Physical development involves the maturation and growth of organs, bones, muscles, and the development of coordination, balance, strength, and motor skills. It also includes the development of sensory systems, such as vision, hearing, taste, touch, and smell. Physical development plays a crucial role in shaping an individual's overall well-being, self-concept, and interaction with the surrounding environment.

sublevels.name: Moral Development
sublevels.description: Moral development, in the field of psychology, refers to the process by which individuals acquire and internalize a sense of right and wrong, develop ethical reasoning abilities, and form their own moral beliefs, values, and behaviors. It involves the progression from a relatively simplistic understanding of morality based on external rules and authority to a more sophisticated understanding that includes consideration of empathy, justice, and the needs and rights of others. Moral development is influenced by various factors, including cognitive, emotional, social, and cultural influences. It is often studied through the lens of moral psychology, examining the development of moral reasoning, moral judgment, moral emotions, and moral behavior across different stages of life.

sublevels.name: Development across Lifespan
sublevels.description: Development across the lifespan is the field of study in psychology that examines the psychological, emotional, and social changes that occur in human beings from birth to old age. This field of study aims to understand how individuals change and develop throughout their lifetime, and how these changes affect their behavior, personality, relationships, and overall well-being. It encompasses a wide range of topics, including physical, cognitive, emotional, and social development, and considers both typical and atypical developmental trajectories. Researchers in this field use a variety of methods, including longitudinal studies, cross-sectional studies, and case studies, to better understand the complexities of development across the lifespan.

sublevels.name: Cognitive Development
sublevels.description: Cognitive development refers to the progressive development and refinement of cognitive abilities such as memory, perception, problem-solving, and decision-making throughout the lifespan. It involves the acquisition and application of knowledge and skills necessary for understanding, interpreting, and interacting with the world. This process is influenced by genetic and environmental factors, and it is often studied in children, although it can also be observed in adults.

sublevels.name: Motor Skills Development
sublevels.description: Motor skills development, in the field of psychology, refers to the progressive acquisition and refinement of physical movements and abilities that involve the coordination of muscles and body parts. It encompasses both gross motor skills, which involve larger muscle groups and whole-body movements, and fine motor skills, which involve precise and coordinated movements of smaller muscle groups, often in the hands and fingers. Motor skills development is a dynamic process that begins in infancy and continues throughout childhood and into adulthood.

sublevels.name: Intelligence Development
sublevels.description: Intelligence development, in the field of psychology, refers to the process through which an individual's cognitive abilities and intellectual functioning evolve and mature over time. It encompasses the acquisition, enhancement, and utilization of cognitive skills, including reasoning, problem-solving, memory, attention, language, and learning. Intelligence development is influenced by a complex interplay of genetic, biological, environmental, and socio-cultural factors. It is not a fixed trait but rather a dynamic and malleable construct that can be shaped and influenced through various experiences, education, and environmental stimuli. Intelligence development is often studied through the examination of individual differences, developmental trajectories, and changes in cognitive abilities across the lifespan.

sublevels.name: Developmental Disabilities
sublevels.description: Developmental disabilities, in the field of psychology, refer to a group of conditions that manifest early in life and result in significant limitations in an individual's cognitive, social, emotional, and physical development. These disabilities are typically chronic and lifelong, and they can affect various aspects of functioning, including intellectual abilities, language and communication skills, motor coordination, and adaptive behavior. Developmental disabilities can arise due to a combination of genetic, environmental, and neurodevelopmental factors.

sublevels.name: Child and Adolescence Psychology
sublevels.description: Child and Adolescent Psychology is a specialized field within psychology that focuses on the study of psychological development and behavior during childhood and adolescence. It examines the cognitive, emotional, social, and physical aspects of development from infancy through adolescence.

sublevels.name: Language Acquisition and Development
sublevels.description: Language acquisition is the ability to understand a language, using it to communicate with others.   Language acquisition and language development can be understood as synonymous

sublevels.name: Psychotherapy
sublevels.description: Psychotherapy is a form of treatment that aims to improve an individual's mental health and well-being by exploring and addressing their psychological and emotional difficulties. It involves the use of various techniques and approaches, such as talk therapy, cognitive-behavioral therapy, and humanistic therapy, to help individuals overcome their problems and improve their quality of life. Psychotherapy is typically conducted by licensed mental health professionals, such as psychologists, psychiatrists, or licensed clinical social workers.

sublevels.name: Psychoanalysis
sublevels.description: Psychoanalysis is a psychological approach and therapeutic method developed by Sigmund Freud that aims to explore and understand unconscious processes, conflicts, and motivations underlying human behavior. It involves the analysis of dreams, free association, and the interpretation of unconscious thoughts and emotions to gain insight into the individual's personality, experiences, and unresolved conflicts. Psychoanalysis focuses on bringing unconscious material into conscious awareness to promote psychological healing and personal growth.

sublevels.name: Therapeutic Relationship
sublevels.description: A therapeutic relationship is a professional and collaborative relationship between a therapist and a client with the goal of promoting the client's well-being and addressing their psychological concerns. It involves building trust, empathy, and rapport between the therapist and the client, as well as maintaining clear boundaries and mutual respect. The therapeutic relationship is a crucial aspect of therapy, as it provides a safe and supportive environment for the client to explore and work through their issues.

sublevels.name: Systems or Family Therapy
sublevels.description: Family therapy, also known as family systems therapy, is an approach in psychology that focuses on understanding and treating psychological issues within the context of family relationships and dynamics. It recognizes that individuals are deeply influenced by their family systems and that addressing the family's interactions and patterns can lead to positive changes in individuals' mental health and well-being. Family therapists work with families to improve communication, resolve conflicts, strengthen relationships, and promote overall family functioning.

sublevels.name: Behaviorial Therapy
sublevels.description: Behavioral therapy, also known as behavior therapy, is an approach within the field of psychology that focuses on modifying and changing problematic behaviors by utilizing principles of learning theory. It is rooted in the belief that behaviors are learned and can be unlearned or replaced with more adaptive behaviors through systematic interventions. Behavioral therapy emphasizes the role of the environment in shaping behavior and utilizes techniques such as positive reinforcement, negative reinforcement, and behavior modification to promote positive change.

sublevels.name: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy
sublevels.description: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) is a widely used therapeutic approach within the field of psychology that focuses on the connections between thoughts, emotions, and behaviors. It is based on the idea that our thoughts and beliefs influence our feelings and behaviors, and by identifying and modifying negative or maladaptive thought patterns, individuals can experience positive changes in their emotions and behaviors. CBT combines cognitive restructuring techniques to address faulty thinking patterns with behavioral techniques to promote behavioral change and improve overall well-being.

sublevels.name: Person-Centered Psychotherapy
sublevels.description: Person-Centered Psychotherapy, also known as Client-Centered Therapy or Rogerian Therapy, is a humanistic approach to psychotherapy developed by Carl Rogers. It emphasizes the importance of the therapeutic relationship and provides a supportive and non-judgmental environment for individuals to explore their feelings, experiences, and self-perceptions. The therapist adopts an empathic and unconditional positive regard towards the client, allowing them to gain self-awareness, self-acceptance, and personal growth.

sublevels.name: Positive Psychology
sublevels.description: Positive psychology focuses on human strengths, like positive mindset, mental well-being, resilience, recovering from bad experiences, and on human propensities as well as conditions to achieve fulfilment and better life experiences.

sublevels.name: Theoretical Psychology
sublevels.description: Theoretical psychology refers to a branch of psychology that is concerned with developing, testing, and refining theories and models of human behavior, mental processes, and experience. Theoretical psychologists often use a range of qualitative and quantitative methods to generate and evaluate hypotheses about psychological phenomena, such as observation, experimentation, simulation, and analysis of discourse, texts, or artifacts. Theoretical psychology draws on insights from various fields, such as philosophy, linguistics, sociology, biology, and computer science, to construct conceptual frameworks and models that can account for the complexity, diversity, and dynamics of psychological phenomena.

sublevels.name: Emotion Theory
sublevels.description: Emotion theory in the field of psychology refers to a collection of theoretical frameworks and models that attempt to explain the nature, function, and development of emotions. Emotions are complex psychological phenomena that involve subjective experiences, physiological changes, cognitive appraisals, expressive behaviors, and social interactions. Emotion theory seeks to provide a systematic and comprehensive understanding of emotions by integrating insights from various fields, such as cognitive psychology, neuroscience, social psychology, and developmental psychology.

sublevels.name: Political Psychology
sublevels.description: Political psychology is a field within psychology that seeks to understand political behavior, attitudes, and decision-making processes. It examines how individuals and groups interact with political institutions and each other, and how factors such as personality, emotions, and social identity influence political behavior. Political psychology also explores the impact of political events, media, and communication on individuals and society, and seeks to develop strategies for promoting democratic values, conflict resolution, and social justice.

sublevels.name: Peace Psychology
sublevels.description: Peace psychology is a subfield of psychology that focuses on understanding the causes of violence and promoting peaceful conflict resolution. It is concerned with the psychological factors that contribute to peace, such as attitudes, beliefs, emotions, and behaviors, as well as the psychological impact of war, terrorism, and other forms of violence on individuals and societies. Peace psychology seeks to develop theories and interventions to promote peace and prevent violence, and it draws on multiple disciplines such as social psychology, political science, sociology, and anthropology to inform its research and practice.

sublevels.name: Psychological Assessment
sublevels.description: Psychological assessment is a field of psychology that involves evaluating and measuring a person's mental, emotional, and behavioral functioning to diagnose and understand psychological issues, determine treatment needs, and evaluate treatment outcomes. It involves the use of various standardized tests, measures, and techniques to gather information about a person's psychological functioning, such as cognitive abilities, personality traits, emotional states, and behavioral patterns. The results of the assessment can be used to develop personalized treatment plans, monitor progress, and inform important decisions in various settings, such as clinical, educational, and forensic contexts.

sublevels.name: Psychological Testing
sublevels.description: Psychological testing refers to the use of standardized and objective methods to measure various aspects of an individual's psychological functioning, including personality traits, cognitive abilities, and emotional states. These tests are designed to provide reliable and valid information about an individual's psychological characteristics, and they are typically administered and interpreted by trained professionals, such as psychologists or psychometricians. Psychological testing can be used in a variety of settings, including clinical assessment, educational and vocational planning, and research.

sublevels.name: Forensic Psychology
sublevels.description: Psychological processes and aspects of court proceedings such as expert reports in criminal, family and social court.

sublevels.name: Economic Psychology
sublevels.description: Economic psychology is a field of study that examines the psychological and behavioral factors that influence economic decisions and behaviors. It applies principles and theories from psychology to better understand how individuals and groups make choices related to financial matters, such as saving, investing, spending, and borrowing. Economic psychology explores how cognitive, emotional, social, and cultural factors impact economic decision-making, and how these factors can be leveraged to improve economic outcomes at the individual, group, and societal levels. It has practical applications in areas such as consumer behavior, marketing, financial planning, public policy, and organizational management.

sublevels.name: Advertising Psychology
sublevels.description: Advertising psychology is a subfield within the broader discipline of consumer behavior that focuses specifically on the psychological processes involved in advertising and marketing. It seeks to understand how consumers perceive, process, and respond to advertising messages, as well as how advertisers can use this information to create more effective and persuasive campaigns.

sublevels.name: Customer Satisfaction
sublevels.description: Customer satisfaction refers to the overall evaluation or assessment that customers make of a product or service they have used or purchased. It is an important construct in the field of consumer behavior, which seeks to understand how consumers think, feel, and behave in relation to different products and services. Customer satisfaction is typically measured through a variety of metrics, including survey-based measures, customer feedback, and online reviews. The goal of measuring customer satisfaction is to identify areas of strengths and weaknesses in a product or service and to use this information to improve customer experiences and build brand loyalty. In addition, customer satisfaction is a key predictor of future consumer behavior, including repeat purchases, recommendations to others, and overall brand engagement.

sublevels.name: Critical Psychology
sublevels.description: Critical Psychology

sublevels.name: Arts
sublevels.description: Art is a diverse range of human activity, and resulting product, that involves creative or imaginative talent expressive of technical proficiency, beauty, emotional power, or conceptual ideas.

sublevels.name: Theatre and Performance Arts
sublevels.description: Theatre is the branch of performing arts concerned with acting out stories in front of an audience, using a combination of speech, gesture, music, dance, sound, and spectacle. Any one or more of these elements is considered performing arts.

sublevels.name: Dance
sublevels.description: Dance is a performing art form consisting of sequences of movement, either improvised or purposefully selected.

sublevels.name: Contemporary Theatre and Performance
sublevels.description: The term contemporary theatre and performance can be defined as a hybrid type body of work that incorporates art, dance, music compositions and more to create a piece of art. Contemporary theatre performance incorporates modern day techniques and embraces thinking outside the box, which allows a much different experience for the audience than just a normal classical piece.

sublevels.name: National and Regional Theatre and Performance
sublevels.description: A regional theater or resident theater in the United States is a professional or semi-professional theater company that produces its own seasons. Forms of theatrical performances Publicistic performance. This stage form is the successor to the action of the once well-known agitribyad. Plastic Choreographic Performance. Dramatic play.  Humorous performance.  Interactive performance.  Performing a forum-theatre. Theatre or theater is a collaborative form of performing art that uses live performers, usually actors or actresses, to present the experience of a real or imagined event before a live audience in a specific place, often a stage.

sublevels.name: Performers and Practitioners
sublevels.description: A practitioner is someone who creates performances and/or produces a theoretical discourse that informs their practical work. Actors or Performers are people who entertain an audience by acting, singing or dancing.

sublevels.name: Applied Theatre
sublevels.description: Applied theatre is an umbrella term that defines theatre which operates beyond the traditional and limiting scope of conventional Western theatre forms.

sublevels.name: Site-Specific Performance
sublevels.description: Site-specific performance is performance created in relation to a physical site and staged at the site itself (as opposed to a theatre space). It often involves research of the site prior to the performance. It is often discussed in relation to both theatre and visual art traditions. Nick Kaye was one of the first scholars to consider site-specific performance from both theatrical and visual art perspectives in his book, Site-Specific Art: Performance, Place and Documentation.

sublevels.name: Theatre History
sublevels.description: The history of theatre is primarily concerned with the origin and subsequent development of the theatre as an autonomous activity. Since classical Athens in the 5th century BC, vibrant traditions of theatre have flourished in cultures across the world.

sublevels.name: Practice-as-Research
sublevels.description: Practice-as-Research (PaR) is an approach to research wherein the main inquiry approach is practice, and the findings of the inquiry are presented through a piece of practice. PaR usually also includes a written outcome, or an archival outcome in other forms (e.g. digital images or lecture recitals), that captures the critical reflection on practice and evidences the new knowledge gained through the process of the practice. PaR is concerned about the nature of practice. It aims to develop knowledge of operational significance and to advance professional work. PaR in a higher education context places emphasis on analysing and theorising practice rather than merely gathering reference materials for the production of an artefact or artwork.

sublevels.name: Global and International Theatre and Performance
sublevels.description: Theatre or theater is a collaborative form of performing art that uses live performers, usually actors or actresses, to present the experience of a real or imagined event before a live audience in a specific place, often a stage.

sublevels.name: Theatre Industry
sublevels.description: The business of theatre and performance.

sublevels.name: Technology and Stagecraft
sublevels.description: StageCraft is an on-set virtual production visual effects technology composed of a video wall designed by Industrial Light & Magic (ILM). Initially developed for the Disney+ series The Mandalorian, it has since been used in other productions and has been cited as a revolutionary visual effects technology.

sublevels.name: Theatre Direction and Production
sublevels.description: Theatrical directing is primarily concerned with the creative aspects of a performance, such as adapting a script for the stage and helping actors embody their characters. A theatrical production is the process involved in conversion of a dramatic text into a theatrical performance which involves a diverse range of art forms from acting, direction, production, lighting, stage props, costume designing, music, backstage support etc.

sublevels.name: Playwrights and Playwriting
sublevels.description: A person who writes plays is a playwright, not a playwrite, but the act of writing plays is usually spelled playwriting. The wright in the compound noun playwright is a little-used word referring to one who constructs or repairs something. It also appears in shipwright, which refers to a person who builds ships.

sublevels.name: Photography
sublevels.description: Photography plays a crucial role in contemporary art. It encompasses and extends across multiple practices. This disregard for a fixed essence is photography’s strength: no aesthetic purity but a range of rhetorical forms used for the creation of fact, fiction and fantasy. Equally the boundary between the still and the moving image is fluid and porous, enabling new forms of image making to be created and disseminated. An informed practice of photography acknowledges the heterogeneous traditions of fine art and visual culture.

sublevels.name: Architecture
sublevels.description: Architecture means the art and practice of designing and making buildings, or the style in which buildings are made.

sublevels.name: Interior Architecture
sublevels.description: Interior architecture is the design of an interior in architectural terms. The interior belongs to a building or shelter and the design serves the interior's functionality for human occupancy.

sublevels.name: Cities, Countries, Regions
sublevels.description: Cities, countries, and regions are geographic entities that play important roles in various contexts, including social, political, economic, and cultural spheres. These terms reflect the diversity of geographical divisions and administrative units across the world. Cities serve as centers of commerce, governance, and cultural exchange, while countries and regions encompass broader territorial boundaries and encompass various cities and rural areas. These entities have distinct identities, histories, and characteristics that shape their social, political, and economic dynamics.

sublevels.name: Architectural History and Theory
sublevels.description: Architectural history traces the changes in architecture through time and space, architectural theory is the act of thinking, discussing, and writing about architecture. The term "architecture" generally refers to buildings, but in its essence is much broader, including fields we now consider specialized forms of practice, such as urbanism, civil engineering, naval, military, and landscape architecture.

sublevels.name: Building Types and Functions
sublevels.description: Building type classifies buildings and architectural constructions along their purposes and functions. Main classes are residential buildings, government buildings, commercial buildings, educational buildings, agricultural buildings or symbolic buildings (e.g. memorial tributes), while needs and functions often overlap.

sublevels.name: Fine Art
sublevels.description: Fine Art is the traditional term used to embrace painting, sculpture and printmaking, produced for its own sake and not concerned with whether it is functional or practical. Recently the term has come to include photography, video and the modern technologies that generate visual imagery.

sublevels.name: Music
sublevels.description: Music is a set of sounds and silences organized into a coherent unit of work such as a scale, an etude, song, a performance, a symphony, or a DJ set.

sublevels.name: Classical Music
sublevels.description: Though "classical music" is the vernacular term, the more accepted academic term is "concert music" or "Western art music." There are many kinds of "classical" musics--e.g., Indian classical music, European classical music--though the term tends to refer primarily to music rooted in the European art music tradition of the 17th-19th centuries.

sublevels.name: Contemporary Music
sublevels.description: Contemporary music typically refers to avant-garde art music of the late 20th and early 21st century; it is sometimes called "New Music."

sublevels.name: History of Music
sublevels.description: Musicology has traditionally focused on the history of music, though in the last 40 years it has expanded to include cultural studies and critical theory methodologies.

sublevels.name: Jazz
sublevels.description: Jazz is a genre of popular music rooted in 20th century African-American urban musical communities and often incorporating improvisation. There are many sub-genres of jazz, including free jazz, fusion, swing, bop and hard bop, neoclassical, etc.

sublevels.name: Music Theatre
sublevels.description: Musical Theatre includes popular and avant-garde theatrical productions and screen musicals that combine acting and singing.

sublevels.name: Pop and Rock
sublevels.description: Pop and Rock refers to both rock-and-roll based popular musics and pop music as a genre that can include but expands beyond rock and roll, often to include a multi-genre mix of music from multiple ethnic and racial groups. The emphasis is commercial rather than underground or indie. When in reference to radio, "pop and rock" generally refers to formats such as "contemporary hits" or "adult hits."

sublevels.name: Popular Music
sublevels.description: Popular music includes music of any genre that has been dubbed or considered popular in any geographic region and at any time in history. It can include pop, rock, EDM, hip hop, folk, blues, jazz, and also things like Broadway musicals and film musicals.

sublevels.name: Theory of Music
sublevels.description: Music Theory focuses on the technical analysis of musical compositions, breaking down their form, harmony, melody, rhythm, timbre, dynamics, and other musical elements. Newer methods include spectrogram analysis and work in music cognition.

sublevels.name: Design
sublevels.description: Design in art refers to the intentional arrangement of visual elements in a work of art. It involves the thoughtful selection and organization of elements such as lines, shapes, colors, textures, and space to create a cohesive and harmonious composition. Design is a crucial aspect of art as it can greatly impact the overall aesthetic appeal and meaning of a work.

sublevels.name: Landscape Architecture
sublevels.description: Landscape Architecture means the systematic design and general engineering of outdoor areas for construction and human use, like for example public parks, parkways, campuses or corporate office parks. It investigates the existing social, ecological, and soil conditions and is therefore a multi-disciplinary field, including aspects of urban design, architecture, geography, ecology, civil engineering, structural engineering, horticulture, environmental psychology, industrial design, soil sciences, botany, and fine arts.

sublevels.name: Interaction Design
sublevels.description: Interaction design, often abbreviated as IxD, is "the practice of designing interactive digital products, environments, systems, and services." While interaction design has an interest in form (similar to other design fields), its main area of focus rests on behavior.

sublevels.name: Graphic Design
sublevels.description: Graphic design is the art and practice of creating visual content to communicate information and ideas to a specific audience. It involves the use of typography, images, and color to convey a message or evoke a certain emotion. Graphic designers use various tools and techniques to create designs for print, digital media, and other visual platforms.

sublevels.name: Industrial Design
sublevels.description: Industrial design (ID) is the professional service of creating and developing concepts and specifications that optimize the function, value and appearance of products and systems for the mutual benefit of both user and manufacturer.

sublevels.name: Contemporary Art
sublevels.description: Contemporary art is the term used for art of the present day. Usually the artists are alive and still making work. Contemporary art is often about ideas and concerns, rather than solely the aesthetic (the look of the work).

sublevels.name: Art History
sublevels.description: Art history is the study of aesthetic objects and visual expression in historical and stylistic context. Since it examines works of art in the context of time, it is adjacent to, but distinguishable from art criticism, art theory and philosophy of art.

sublevels.name: Theory of Arts
sublevels.description: Scholarship in theory of arts studies questions related to what art (or music, or dance, etc.) is, what creativity is, what an artwork is, the relationship between art and society or art and the subject, how art is valued and evaluated, etc.

sublevels.name: Economics
sublevels.description: Economics is the study of how people allocate scarce resources for production, distribution, and consumption, both individually and collectively. The two branches of economics are microeconomics and macroeconomics. Economics focuses on efficiency in production and exchange.

sublevels.name: International Economics
sublevels.description: International economics is concerned with the effects upon economic activity from international differences in productive resources and consumer preferences and the international institutions that affect them. It seeks to explain the patterns and consequences of transactions and interactions between the inhabitants of different countries, including trade, investment and transaction.

sublevels.name: European Economic Integration
sublevels.description: European integration is the process of industrial, economic, political, legal, social, and cultural integration of states wholly or partially in Europe or nearby. European integration has primarily come about through the European Union and its policies.  In practical terms, EMU means: Coordination of economic policy-making between Member States. Coordination of fiscal policies, notably through limits on government debt and deficit. An independent monetary policy run by the European Central Bank (ECB).

sublevels.name: International Finance
sublevels.description: International finance is a field of study and practice that focuses on the financial interactions between countries and multinational corporations operating across borders. It involves analyzing the flows of money and capital across international borders, assessing the risks associated with those flows, and devising strategies to manage those risks.  Some major topics in international finance include:  Foreign exchange rates, Transfer pricing: The study of foreign exchange rates is an important part of international finance. This involves understanding the factors that influence exchange rates, such as interest rates, inflation, and political events.  International investment: International investment involves analyzing the risks and opportunities associated with investing in foreign countries. This may include examining the political and economic conditions in a given country, as well as evaluating the legal and regulatory environment.  Capital flows: The movement of capital between countries is a crucial part of international finance. This includes analyzing the flows of foreign direct investment (FDI), portfolio investments, and other forms of capital.  International trade finance: International trade finance involves the financing and management of international trade transactions, including the provision of credit, insurance, and other financial services.  International banking: International banking involves analyzing the operations of multinational banks, as well as examining the regulatory and supervisory frameworks that govern these institutions.  Multinational corporations: Multinational corporations (MNCs) play a major role in international finance. Analyzing the financial strategies of MNCs, as well as the risks associated with their operations in different countries, is an important topic in the field.  International financial markets: The study of international financial markets involves examining the operations of stock, bond, and other financial markets in different countries, as well as evaluating the risks and opportunities associated with investing in these markets.

sublevels.name: International Trade
sublevels.description: International trade is the exchange of capital, goods, and services across international borders or territories because there is a need or want of goods or services. (see: World economy) In most countries, such trade represents a significant share of gross domestic product (GDP).

sublevels.name: Economic Aspects of Globalization
sublevels.description: Economic globalization refers to the increasing interdependence of world economies as a result of the growing scale of cross-border trade of commodities and services, flow of international capital and wide and rapid spread of technologies. In general, globalization decreases the cost of manufacturing. This means that companies can offer goods at a lower price to consumers. The average cost of goods is a key aspect that contributes to increases in the standard of living. Consumers also have access to a wider variety of goods. The characteristic elements that constitute economic globalization are cross-border flows of goods and services, capital, people, data and ideas

sublevels.name: Sector and Industry Studies
sublevels.description: Sector analysis is an assessment of the economic and financial condition and prospects of a given sector of the economy. Sector analysis serves to provide an investor with a judgment about how well companies in the sector are expected to perform. Industry refers to a group of companies that operate in a similar business sphere, and its categorization is narrow. Sector refers to a part of the economy into which various industries consisting of a great number of companies can be fit, and is larger in comparison.

sublevels.name: Real Estate Economics
sublevels.description: Real estate economics is the application of economic techniques to real estate markets. It tries to describe, explain, and predict patterns of prices, supply, and demand.

sublevels.name: Tourism Economics
sublevels.description: Tourism economics is a branch of applied economics that studies the economic impacts of tourism and tourism activity.

sublevels.name: Cultural Economics
sublevels.description: Cultural economics is the branch of economics that studies the relation of culture to economic outcomes.

sublevels.name: Public Sector Studies
sublevels.description: Public sector studies include the studies on public goods and governmental services such as the military, law enforcement, infrastructure, public transit, public education, along with health care and those working for the government itself, such as elected officials.

sublevels.name: Sports Economics
sublevels.description: Sports Economics is the study of issues of sports by means of economics, its methods and theoretical frameworks (heavily based on macroeconomics) as well as the study of economics problems in the context of sports. Sports Economics attempts to describe, explain and prognosticate actions by relevant parties and use the acquired knowledge technologically.

sublevels.name: Transportation Economics
sublevels.description: Transportation economics is the study of allocation of resources within the transport sector. It deals with economic structures of different transport systems, their socio-economic impact, demand and supply of transports, different transport models and the study of their capacity, effectiveness, frequency, environment and financing; cost benefit analysis, public and commercial transport planning, economics of and investments in transport infrastructure projects, transport data analytics, and transportation policy.

sublevels.name: Maritime Economics
sublevels.description: Maritime economics explains trade and economic aspects of commercial shipping, port operations, and how different types of shipping markets are organized and works, including demand and supply variations, reasons for sea transport, organization of sea transport, transport of bulk, general, merchant & specialized cargo, prices and freight rates determination, ship finance, market cycles, shipping companies risk and return on investment, how shipping company survive depressions, drivers in ship design, market forecasts, and environmental costs.

sublevels.name: Education Economics
sublevels.description: Education economics, or the economics of education, is the study of economic issues relating to education, including the demand for education, the financing and provision of education, and the comparative efficiency of various educational programs and policies.

sublevels.name: Health Economics
sublevels.description: Health economics is a branch of economics concerned with issues related to efficiency, effectiveness, value and behavior in the production and consumption of health and healthcare.

sublevels.name: Public Economics
sublevels.description: Public economics (or economics of the public sector) is the study of government policy through the lens of economic efficiency and equity. Public economics builds on the theory of welfare economics and is ultimately used as a tool to improve social welfare. Welfare can be defined in terms of well-being, prosperity, and overall state of being.

sublevels.name: Public Choice and Political Economy
sublevels.description: Public choice, or public choice theory, is "the use of economic tools to deal with traditional problems of political science". Its content includes the study of political behavior. In political science, it is the subset of positive political theory that studies self-interested agents (voters, politicians, bureaucrats) and their interactions, which can be represented in a number of ways – using (for example) standard constrained utility maximization, game theory, or decision theory. Political economy approaches in general contend that the success or failure of public policies depends on political struggles, or the ability to neutralise political struggles, around resources.

sublevels.name: Voting
sublevels.description: Voting is when a group of people decide something by saying what they want. It can be for electing a leader or representative, passing a law, and other things. When people are done voting, the votes are counted (often by machines) and the winner is determined.

sublevels.name: Public Finance
sublevels.description: Public finance is the study of the role of the government in the economy. It is the branch of economics that assesses the government revenue and government expenditure of the public authorities and the adjustment of one or the other to achieve desirable effects and avoid undesirable ones. The purview of public finance is considered to be threefold, consisting of governmental effects on: 1.	The efficient allocation of available resources; 2.	The distribution of income among citizens; and 3.	The stability of the economy.

sublevels.name: Fiscal Policy
sublevels.description: Tax policy refers to the guidelines and principles established by a government for the imposition and collection of taxes. It encompasses both microeconomic and macroeconomic aspects, with the former focusing on issues of fairness and efficiency in tax collection, and the latter focusing on the overall quantity of taxes to be collected and its impact on economic activity. The tax framework of a country is considered a crucial instrument for influencing the country's economy.

sublevels.name: Taxation Policy
sublevels.description: Tax policy refers to the guidelines and principles established by a government for the imposition and collection of taxes. It encompasses both microeconomic and macroeconomic aspects, with the former focusing on issues of fairness and efficiency in tax collection, and the latter focusing on the overall quantity of taxes to be collected and its impact on economic activity. The tax framework of a country is considered a crucial instrument for influencing the country's economy.

sublevels.name: Regulation and Industrial Policy
sublevels.description: Industrial policy can be defined as a statement stating the role of government in industrial development, the position of public and private sectors in industrialization of the country, the comparative role of large and small industries.

sublevels.name: Socio-Economic Policy
sublevels.description: Social policy is concerned with the ways societies across the world meet human needs for security, education, work, health and wellbeing. Social policy addresses how states and societies respond to global challenges of social, demographic and economic change, and of poverty, migration and globalisation. Social policy is a plan or action of government or institutional agencies which aim to improve or reform society. The economy of governments covers the systems for setting levels of taxation, government budgets, the money supply and interest rates as well as the labour market, national ownership, and many other areas of government interventions into the economy.

sublevels.name: Social Economy
sublevels.description: The term 'social economy' refers to all business activities that are not only driven by a strong social mission but also intended to be economically viable.

sublevels.name: Public Administration
sublevels.description: The study of the implementation of government policies.

sublevels.name: e-Governance
sublevels.description: E-government refers to the use of the ICTs in public administration which, when combined with organizational change and new skills, are intended to improve public services and democratic processes and to strengthen support to the public.

sublevels.name: Economic Policy
sublevels.description: The economy of governments covers the systems for setting levels of taxation, government budgets, the money supply and interest rates as well as the labour market, national ownership, and many other areas of government interventions into the economy.  Most factors of economic policy can be divided into either fiscal policy, which deals with government actions regarding taxation and spending, or monetary policy, which deals with central banking actions regarding the money supply and interest rates.

sublevels.name: Public Administration
sublevels.description: The study of the implementation of government policies.

sublevels.name: e-Governance
sublevels.description: E-government refers to the use of the ICTs in public administration which, when combined with organizational change and new skills, are intended to improve public services and democratic processes and to strengthen support to the public.

sublevels.name: Microeconomics
sublevels.description: Microeconomics is a branch of mainstream economics that studies the behavior of individuals and firms in making decisions regarding the allocation of scarce resources and the interactions among these individuals and firms.

sublevels.name: Social Choice and Welfare
sublevels.description: Social Choice and Welfare studies the methods and principles for aggregating individual preferences and making collective decisions, focusing on issues of fairness, efficiency, and social welfare.

sublevels.name: Voting
sublevels.description: Voting is when a group of people decide something by saying what they want. It can be for electing a leader or representative, passing a law, and other things. When people are done voting, the votes are counted (often by machines) and the winner is determined.

sublevels.name: Welfare
sublevels.description: The term welfare refers to a range of government programs that provide financial or other aid to individuals or groups who cannot support themselves. Welfare programs are typically funded by taxpayers and allow people to cope with financial stress during rough periods of their lives.

sublevels.name: General Equilibrium
sublevels.description: General equilibrium shows how supply and demand interact and tend toward a balance in an economy of multiple markets working at once. The balance of competing levels of supply and demand in different markets ultimately creates a price equilibrium.

sublevels.name: Market Structure and Economic Design
sublevels.description: According to economic theory, market structure describes how firms are differentiated and categorized by the types of products they sell and how those items influence their operations. A market structure helps us to understand what differentiates markets from one another. Review of Economic Design comprises the creative art and science of inventing, analyzing and testing economic as well as social and political institutions and mechanisms aimed at achieving individual objectives and social goals.

sublevels.name: Economy-wide Country Studies
sublevels.description: Macroeconomics is a branch of economics that deals with the performance, structure, behavior, and decision-making of an economy as a whole—for example, using interest rates, taxes, and government spending to regulate an economy's growth and stability. This includes regional, national, and global economies.   Macroeconomists study topics such as GDP (Gross Domestic Product), unemployment (including unemployment rates), national income, price indices, output, consumption, inflation, saving, investment, energy, international trade, and international finance.

sublevels.name: Asian Economics
sublevels.description: The economy of Asia comprises about 4.7 billion people (60% of the world population) living in 50 different nations. Asia is the fastest growing economic region, as well as the largest continental economy by both GDP Nominal and PPP in the world.

sublevels.name: Middle Eastern/North African Economics
sublevels.description: Middle East and Northern Africa (MENA) encompasses the countries between Iran in the East and Tunisia and Morocco in the West. According to OPEC data, the MENA region holds more than half of the world's oil reserves, and two-fifths of the world's natural gas reserves. Due to the region's substantial petroleum and natural gas production, MENA is an important source of global economic and energy resources.

sublevels.name: Latin American/Caribbean Economics
sublevels.description: Latin America as a region has multiple nation-states, with varying levels of economic complexity. The Latin American economy is an export-based economy consisting of individual countries in the geographical regions of North America, Central America, South America, and the Caribbean.

sublevels.name: North American Economics
sublevels.description: The economy of North America comprises more than 596 million people (8% of the world population) in its 24 sovereign states and 15 dependent territories. It is marked by a sharp division between the predominantly English speaking countries of Canada and the United States, which are among the wealthiest and most developed nations in the world, and countries of Central America and the Caribbean in the former Latin America that are less developed. Mexico and Caribbean nations of the Commonwealth of Nations are between the economic extremes of the development of North America.

sublevels.name: African Economics
sublevels.description: Africa makes up around 20% of the earth's landmass, and is home to approximately 16% of the world's population. Nevertheless, Africa's economies account for just 3% of the world's GDP. In the past, economic ties between African nations and strong economies outside of Africa have been fundamentally exploitative.

sublevels.name: European Economics
sublevels.description: The economy of Europe comprises about 748 million people in 50 countries. The formation of the European Union (EU) and in 1999 the introduction of a unified currency, the Euro, brought participating European countries closer through the convenience of a shared currency and has led to a stronger European cash flow. The European Union is a unique global organisation, an entity forming one of the largest economies in the world. The European Union also “regulates” the global market by the single market.

sublevels.name: Industrial Organization
sublevels.description: Industrial organization is an analysis of factors, operational or otherwise, that contribute to a firm's overall strategy and product placement. It involves a study of different areas, from market power to product differentiation to industrial policy, that affect a firm's operations.

sublevels.name: Regulation and Industrial Policy
sublevels.description: Industrial policy can be defined as a statement stating the role of government in industrial development, the position of public and private sectors in industrialization of the country, the comparative role of large and small industries.

sublevels.name: Market Structure and Economic Design
sublevels.description: According to economic theory, market structure describes how firms are differentiated and categorized by the types of products they sell and how those items influence their operations. A market structure helps us to understand what differentiates markets from one another. Review of Economic Design comprises the creative art and science of inventing, analyzing and testing economic as well as social and political institutions and mechanisms aimed at achieving individual objectives and social goals.

sublevels.name: Economic History
sublevels.description: Economic history is the study of history using methodological tools from economics or with a special attention to economic phenomena.

sublevels.name: Financial History
sublevels.description: Financial History studies the development of financial systems, institutions, and markets over time, including the evolution of banking, investment, and monetary policies.

sublevels.name: Financial Crises
sublevels.description: A financial crisis is any of a broad variety of situations in which some financial assets suddenly lose a large part of their nominal value.

sublevels.name: History of Economic Thought and Methodology
sublevels.description: Research in the History of Economic Thought and Methodology (RHETM) is a journal/book series dedicated to an interdisciplinary approach to a broad range of topics related to the history and methodology of economics.

sublevels.name: Corporate History
sublevels.description: A corporate history is a historical account of a business or other co-operative organization. Usually it is produced in written format but it can also be published as audio or audiovisually.

sublevels.name: Quantitative Economics
sublevels.description: Quantitative economics is analyzis of economic issues, explore theories, and predict future conditions using statistical procedures and mathematical models.

sublevels.name: Experimental Economics
sublevels.description: Experimental Economics uses controlled experiments to study economic behavior and test economic theories, providing empirical insights into decision-making processes and market dynamics.

sublevels.name: Computational Economics
sublevels.description: Computational Economics is a field of research in which economists and computer scientists use software-based methods to solve analytical problems in order to make accurate predictions about the economy.

sublevels.name: Game Theory
sublevels.description: Game theory is the study of mathematical models of strategic interaction between rational decision-makers. It has applications in all fields of social science, as well as in logic and computer science. Originally, it addressed zero-sum games, in which one person's gains result in losses for the other participants. Today, game theory applies to a wide range of behavioral relations, and is now an umbrella term for the science of logical decision making in humans, animals, and computers

sublevels.name: Econometrics
sublevels.description: Econometrics is the application of statistical and mathematical methods to economic data. It aims to quantify economic relationships, test economic theories, and forecast future economic trends. By using statistical tools, econometrics helps in making informed decisions and policies based on empirical data. It combines economic theory, mathematics, and statistical inference to analyze economic phenomena.

sublevels.name: Financial Econometrics
sublevels.description: Financial econometrics is the application of statistical methods to financial market data. Financial econometrics is a branch of financial economics, in the field of economics. Areas of study include capital markets, financial institutions, corporate finance and corporate governance. Topics often revolve around asset valuation of individual stocks, bonds, derivatives, currencies and other financial instruments.

sublevels.name: Time Series Analysis
sublevels.description: A time series is a sequence of measurements performed at successive points in time. Time series can be used to derive models to predict future values based on previously observed values. Time series are used in statistics, signal processing, pattern recognition, econometrics, mathematical finance, weather forecasting, earthquake prediction, electroencephalography, control engineering, astronomy, communications engineering, and largely in any domain of applied science and engineering which involves temporal measurements

sublevels.name: Macroeconomics and Monetary Economics
sublevels.description: Monetary economics is the branch of economics that studies the different theories of money: it provides a framework for analyzing money and considers its functions (such as medium of exchange, store of value, and unit of account), and it considers how money can gain acceptance purely because of its convenience as a public good. The discipline has historically prefigured, and remains integrally linked to, macroeconomics. This branch also examines the effects of monetary systems, including regulation of money and associated financial institutions and international aspects.  Modern analysis has attempted to provide microfoundations for the demand for money and to distinguish valid nominal and real monetary relationships for micro or macro uses, including their influence on the aggregate demand for output. Its methods include deriving and testing the implications of money as a substitute for other assets and as based on explicit frictions.

sublevels.name: Regional Economics
sublevels.description: Regional Economics refer to the economic advantage of a geographical location and human activities of greatest height to contribute maximally to the general growth and prosperity of the region. Spatial economics is the study of how space (distance) affects economic behavior.

sublevels.name: Spatial Economics
sublevels.description: Spatial Economics studies the allocation of resources and economic activities across different locations, focusing on factors such as transportation, land use, and regional development.

sublevels.name: Urban Economics
sublevels.description: Urban Economics studies the economic functions and development of cities, focusing on issues such as land use, housing, transportation, and urban policy.

sublevels.name: Heterodox Economics
sublevels.description: Heterodox economics is any economic thought or theory that contrasts with orthodox schools of economic thought, or that may be beyond neoclassical economics.

sublevels.name: Institutional and Evolutionary Economics
sublevels.description: Institutional economics focuses on understanding the role of the evolutionary process and the role of institutions in shaping economic behavior. Its original focus lay in Thorstein Veblen's instinct-oriented dichotomy between technology on the one side and the "ceremonial" sphere of society on the other. Evolutionary economics is a theory proposing that economic processes evolve and that economic behavior is determined both by individuals and society as a whole. The term was first coined by Thorstein Veblen (1857-1929), an American economist and sociologist.

sublevels.name: Agent-based Economics
sublevels.description: Agent-based computational economics (ACE) is the area of computational economics that studies economic processes, including whole economies, as dynamic systems of interacting agents. As such, it falls in the paradigm of complex adaptive systems.

sublevels.name: Feminist Economics
sublevels.description: Feminist economics is the critical study of economics and economies, with a focus on gender-aware and inclusive economic inquiry and policy analysis. Feminist economic researchers include academics, activists, policy theorists, and practitioners. Much feminist economic research focuses on topics that have been neglected in the field, such as care work, intimate partner violence, or on economic theories which could be improved through better incorporation of gendered effects and interactions, such as between paid and unpaid sectors of economies.

sublevels.name: Marxist Economics
sublevels.description: Marxian economics is a school of economic thought based on the work of 19th-century economist and philosopher Karl Marx. Marxian economics, or Marxist economics, focuses on the role of labor in the development of an economy and is critical of the classical approach to wages and productivity developed by Adam Smith.

sublevels.name: Demographic Economics
sublevels.description: Demographic economics is the use of population data as a way to study the patterns of behavior among groups of people that impact the economy. This is also why it is known as population economics. Demographics are statistics about groups of people that help to identify groups for tracking and research purposes.

sublevels.name: Gender Economics
sublevels.description: Gender economics is the study of how gender affects individuals' economic behavior, opportunities, and outcomes, incorporating the analysis of the impact of gender roles, discrimination, and policies on labor markets, income distribution, and resource allocation.

sublevels.name: Economics of Migration
sublevels.description: Economics of Migration studies the economic causes and consequences of migration, including the impact on labor markets, economic growth, and the distribution of resources.

sublevels.name: Behavioral Economics
sublevels.description: Behavioral Economics is the study of psychology as it relates to the economic decision-making processes of individuals and institutions. Behavioral economics is often related with normative economics. It draws on psychology and economics to explore why people sometimes make irrational decisions, and why and how their behavior does not follow the predictions of economic models.

sublevels.name: Behavioral Finance
sublevels.description: Define behavioral finance as in research and practice Behavioral finance is an interdisciplinary field of study that combines principles of psychology and economics to understand how human behavior and emotions influence financial decisions and markets. In research and practice, behavioral finance aims to explain why people make irrational financial decisions, and how these decisions impact markets and the economy as a whole.  Behavioral finance researchers study various psychological and cognitive biases that affect financial decision-making, such as overconfidence, loss aversion, and herding behavior. They also examine the role of emotions, social norms, and cultural factors in shaping financial attitudes and behaviors.  In practice, behavioral finance is used to develop strategies and tools for improving financial decision-making and investment outcomes. This may include developing investment products that take into account investors' behavioral tendencies and preferences, or designing financial education programs that aim to overcome common cognitive biases and promote rational decision-making.  Overall, behavioral finance seeks to provide a more complete understanding of financial markets and investor behavior, with the goal of improving investment outcomes and reducing financial risk.

sublevels.name: Political Economy and Economic Systems
sublevels.description: Political economy is an interdisciplinary branch of the social sciences. It focuses on the interrelationships of individuals, governments, and public policy. Political economists study how economic theories such as capitalism, socialism, and communism work in the real world. A political-economic system can be defined as the relationship between political and economic institutions in a particular country, as well as their policies. Market, command, and mixed economies are all examples of economic systems, and each of those can easily be influenced by politics.

sublevels.name: History of Economic Thought and Methodology
sublevels.description: Research in the History of Economic Thought and Methodology (RHETM) is a journal/book series dedicated to an interdisciplinary approach to a broad range of topics related to the history and methodology of economics.

sublevels.name: Transitional Economics
sublevels.description: The study of economies that move from one economic system to another. This is an area of study that developed following the end of the Soviet Union and the shift from centrally planned economies to market economies seen within the ex-Soviet states. Other countries that have also shifted economic systems, such as China and countries in South America, have also been areas of focus.

sublevels.name: Political Economy of Energy
sublevels.description: Political Economy of Energy studies all aspects of energy in relation to law, customs and government.

sublevels.name: Financial Economics
sublevels.description: Financial economics, also known as finance, is the branch of economics characterized by a "concentration on monetary activities", in which "money of one type or another is likely to appear on both sides of a trade". Its concern is thus the interrelation of financial variables, such as share prices, interest rates and exchange rates, as opposed to those concerning the real economy. It has two main areas of focus: asset pricing, commonly known as "Investments", and corporate finance; the first being the perspective of providers of capital, i.e. investors, and the second of users of capital. It thus provides the theoretical underpinning for much of finance.  The subject is concerned with "the allocation and deployment of economic resources, both spatially and across time, in an uncertain environment". It, therefore, centers on decision-making under uncertainty in the context of the financial markets, and the resultant economic and financial models and principles, and is concerned with deriving testable or policy implications from acceptable assumptions. It is built on the foundations of microeconomics and decision theory.  Financial econometrics is the branch of financial economics that uses econometric techniques to parameterize these relationships.

sublevels.name: Financial Services
sublevels.description: The financial services industry is a broad field of business and management research that encompasses organizations and institutions involved in the provision of financial products and services to clients. This includes banking, insurance, investment management, and other financial intermediation services. Research in this field may focus on the structure and organization of financial institutions, regulatory frameworks, financial markets and instruments, risk management, and the impact of technology and innovation on the industry. It may also explore the behavior of financial consumers and their decision-making processes, as well as the economic and social implications of financial services for individuals, businesses, and societies.

sublevels.name: Insurance
sublevels.description: The insurance industry is a field of business and management research that focuses on the study of the insurance sector. This includes the analysis of various types of insurance products such as life insurance, health insurance, property and casualty insurance, and other specialized insurance products. Research in this field covers a range of topics, including the regulation of the industry, risk management, underwriting, claims processing, and actuarial science. Additionally, research may examine the impact of emerging technologies on the industry, the use of big data and analytics, and the role of insurance in broader economic and social contexts.

sublevels.name: Investments and Securities
sublevels.description: The Investments and Securities industry is a field of business and management research that focuses on the analysis, management, and trading of financial instruments such as stocks, bonds, options, and other securities. The field encompasses a wide range of topics, including portfolio management, risk management, financial analysis, asset pricing, trading strategies, and market microstructure. It involves understanding the behavior of financial markets and the factors that influence their movements, as well as developing models and tools to help investors make informed decisions about their investments. Research in this field often involves the use of quantitative methods and may draw upon insights from economics, finance, and mathematics.

sublevels.name: Banking
sublevels.description: The banking industry is a field of business and management research that focuses on financial institutions that provide various banking services to individuals, businesses, and governments. It includes the study of banking operations, financial management, risk management, corporate governance, regulations, and innovations in the banking sector. Some of the key topics in banking industry research include the impact of technology on banking, financial regulation and compliance, financial risk management, asset and liability management, investment banking, retail banking, and financial inclusion. The banking industry is a critical component of the global economy, and research in this field can provide insights into economic growth, financial stability, and sustainable development.

sublevels.name: Capital Markets
sublevels.description: A capital market is a financial market in which long-term debt (over a year) or equity-backed securities are bought and sold, in contrast to a money market where short-term debt is bought and sold. Capital markets channel the wealth of savers to those who can put it to long-term productive use, such as companies or governments making long-term investments.

sublevels.name: Financial Crises
sublevels.description: A financial crisis is any of a broad variety of situations in which some financial assets suddenly lose a large part of their nominal value.

sublevels.name: Behavioral Finance
sublevels.description: Define behavioral finance as in research and practice Behavioral finance is an interdisciplinary field of study that combines principles of psychology and economics to understand how human behavior and emotions influence financial decisions and markets. In research and practice, behavioral finance aims to explain why people make irrational financial decisions, and how these decisions impact markets and the economy as a whole.  Behavioral finance researchers study various psychological and cognitive biases that affect financial decision-making, such as overconfidence, loss aversion, and herding behavior. They also examine the role of emotions, social norms, and cultural factors in shaping financial attitudes and behaviors.  In practice, behavioral finance is used to develop strategies and tools for improving financial decision-making and investment outcomes. This may include developing investment products that take into account investors' behavioral tendencies and preferences, or designing financial education programs that aim to overcome common cognitive biases and promote rational decision-making.  Overall, behavioral finance seeks to provide a more complete understanding of financial markets and investor behavior, with the goal of improving investment outcomes and reducing financial risk.

sublevels.name: Statistical Finance
sublevels.description: Statistical Finance applies statistical methods and models to analyze and predict financial markets, asset prices, and economic trends.

sublevels.name: Investments and Securities
sublevels.description: The Investments and Securities industry is a field of business and management research that focuses on the analysis, management, and trading of financial instruments such as stocks, bonds, options, and other securities. The field encompasses a wide range of topics, including portfolio management, risk management, financial analysis, asset pricing, trading strategies, and market microstructure. It involves understanding the behavior of financial markets and the factors that influence their movements, as well as developing models and tools to help investors make informed decisions about their investments. Research in this field often involves the use of quantitative methods and may draw upon insights from economics, finance, and mathematics.

sublevels.name: Financial Econometrics
sublevels.description: Financial econometrics is the application of statistical methods to financial market data. Financial econometrics is a branch of financial economics, in the field of economics. Areas of study include capital markets, financial institutions, corporate finance and corporate governance. Topics often revolve around asset valuation of individual stocks, bonds, derivatives, currencies and other financial instruments.

sublevels.name: Resource and Environmental Economics
sublevels.description: Environmental and resource economics, a specialization option in the economic sciences major, applies economic and management decision tools to issues in forest management, water use, pollution, land use, fisheries, recycling, and hazardous wastes.

sublevels.name: Agricultural Economics
sublevels.description: Agricultural economics is an applied field of economics concerned with the application of economic theory in optimizing the production and distribution of food and fiber products. It involves studying the economic aspects of agricultural activities, including farming, food production, agribusiness, rural development, and natural resource management. Agricultural economists analyze and evaluate factors that influence agricultural markets, policies, and decision-making at various levels, from individual farms to national and international agricultural systems.

sublevels.name: Natural Resource Economics
sublevels.description: Natural Resource Economics is the study of how societies use and manage the Earth's natural resources—such as water, minerals, forests, and energy—in ways that balance economic needs with environmental sustainability.

sublevels.name: Environmental Economics
sublevels.description: Environmental economics is the study of the economics of ecological and environmental issues. It focuses on the monetary value of ecosystems and the costs and benefits of environmental policies.

sublevels.name: Energy Economics
sublevels.description: Energy economics studies human utilization of energy resources and the consequences of that utilization.

sublevels.name: Economic Development, Innovation and Growth
sublevels.description: Innovation has led to increased productivity even as the workweek became shorter and production less capital intensive over the last two centuries.
