Rather than viewing the history of philosophy as a separate discipline or a mere historical survey, this approach considers it as an active and integral part of philosophical investigation.

sublevels.name: Logical Analysis
sublevels.description: Logical analysis refers to the systematic examination and evaluation of arguments and propositions using the principles and methods of logic. It involves breaking down complex statements or arguments into their logical components to assess their validity, soundness, consistency, and coherence. Logical analysis aims to uncover the logical structure of a statement or argument and determine whether it follows valid reasoning.

sublevels.name: Mathematical Logic in Philosophy
sublevels.description: Mathematical logic, also known as symbolic logic or formal logic, plays a crucial role in philosophy as a tool for rigorous analysis and investigation of philosophical concepts and arguments. It is a branch of logic that uses mathematical methods and symbolic notation to study formal systems of reasoning.

sublevels.name: World Philosophy
sublevels.description: World Philosophy is the comparative study of philosophical traditions and ideas from various cultural and historical contexts, aiming to promote understanding and dialogue between different intellectual systems and perspectives.

sublevels.name: Postcolonial Philosophy
sublevels.description: Postcolonial Philosophy arose in the 20th century as a methodology and tradition for thinking critically about the afterlives of colonialism and its ongoing impacts on the Global South.

sublevels.name: Philosophical Anthropology
sublevels.description: Philosophical anthropology is a branch of philosophy that examines fundamental questions about human nature, existence, and the essence of what it means to be human. It explores the nature of human beings, their place in the world, their relationships with others, and their search for meaning and purpose. Philosophical anthropology is an interdisciplinary field that draws from philosophy, anthropology, psychology, sociology, and other disciplines.

sublevels.name: Philosophy of Religion
sublevels.description: Philosophy of Religion explores fundamental questions about religion, including the nature and existence of deities, the problem of evil, and the relationship between faith and reason.

sublevels.name: Philosophy of History
sublevels.description: Philosophy or history; nature of history; Or The philosophy of history is a branch of philosophy that explores the nature, purpose, and interpretation of history. It examines fundamental questions about the nature of historical knowledge, the role of individuals and societies in shaping historical events, and the broader patterns or themes that emerge throughout human history.

sublevels.name: Kulturphilosophie
sublevels.description: Self-assessment ("Selbsteinschätzung") of man as a cultural being; problem areas: the idea of a development of man ("Kultivierung") and his epistemic achievements; origins in Romanticism; overlaps with Philosophical Anthropology; i.a. in the context of Schelling, Herder, Humboldt; Schiller, Kant; Spengler, Cassirer, Simmel; thematic areas: the relation of culture and nature; productivity; cultural criticism

sublevels.name: Cultural Studies
sublevels.description: Cultural studies, also called the cultural sciences, is an interdisciplinary field or scientific branch that examines the dynamics of contemporary culture (including its politics and popular culture) and its historical foundations.

sublevels.name: Popular Culture
sublevels.description: The academic study of popular culture encompassing diverse media such as film, television, and comic books, combining communication and cultural studies.

sublevels.name: Comics Studies
sublevels.description: Comics studies is an academic field that focuses on comics & graphic novels, and sequential art.

sublevels.name: Gothic Studies
sublevels.description: The study of Gothic—includes literature, film, popular culture and any other mode of gothic.

sublevels.name: Fashion and the Body
sublevels.description: Fashion and the body investigates how fashion has influenced bodily practice, and culture. It explores modes of representation that fashion has taken historically, but also considers the cultural contexts for new directions, at a time when the fashioned body is increasingly implicated in the negotiation of individual and collective identities.

sublevels.name: Games Studies
sublevels.description: Games studies is an interdisciplinary field of academic study that focuses on the analysis, interpretation, and understanding of games and gaming culture. It encompasses various aspects of games, including their design, mechanics, aesthetics, social and cultural impact, and player experiences.

sublevels.name: Youth Culture
sublevels.description: Youth culture refers to the cultural practice of members of this age group by which they express their identities and demonstrate their sense of belonging to a particular group of young people.

sublevels.name: Celebrity Studies
sublevels.description: Celebrity studies is the critical exploration of celebrity, stardom and fame. It seeks to make sense of celebrity by drawing upon a range of (inter)disciplinary approaches, media forms, historical periods and national contexts.

sublevels.name: Fan and Audience Studies
sublevels.description: Fan studies is an academic discipline that analyses fans, fandoms, fan cultures and fan activities, including fanworks. It draws particularly on audience studies and cultural studies.

sublevels.name: Comedy Studies
sublevels.description: The academic study of comedy and its cultural significance

sublevels.name: Sound Studies
sublevels.description: Sound Studies is an interdisciplinary field exploring the cultural, historical, and technological dimensions of sound and listening. It examines how practices like voice, noise, silence, and aural perception are shaped by society and media, with an emphasis on sound reproduction technologies.

sublevels.name: Medical Humanities
sublevels.description: Medical Humanities is an interdisciplinary field that explores the intersection of medicine, arts, and humanities, aiming to enhance the understanding of the human experience in healthcare.

sublevels.name: Cultural Heritage
sublevels.description: Cultural heritage is the legacy of cultural resources and intangible attributes of a group or society that is inherited from past generations. Not all legacies of past generations are "heritage", rather heritage is a product of selection by society.

sublevels.name: Cultural Policy and Politics
sublevels.description: Cultural policy is the government actions, laws and programs that regulate, protect, encourage and financially (or otherwise) support activities related to the arts and creative sectors, such as painting, sculpture, music, dance, literature, and filmmaking, among others and culture, which may involve activities related to language, heritage and diversity. Cultural politics is an analytical framing of politics in society that recognizes “the cultural” as a vital site for political struggles over meaning, wherein different societal groups negotiate questions about identity, belonging, inclusion, and exclusion.

sublevels.name: Museology
sublevels.description: Museum studies is the study of museums. It explores the history of museums and their role in society, as well as the activities they engage in, including curating, preservation, public programming, and education.

sublevels.name: Cultural Management
sublevels.description: Cultural management refers to the professional planning, organization, and control of cultural activities and institutions. It encompasses strategic development, financing, personnel management, marketing, as well as the operational management of cultural projects, facilities, or events with the aim of efficiently utilizing cultural resources and making cultural content accessible to a (broad) audience. Central reference disciplines include business administration management theory, cultural and theatre studies, cultural policy, cultural sociology, and cultural economics.

sublevels.name: Visual Culture
sublevels.description: Visual Culture studies the role and impact of visual images and media in society, exploring how visual representations shape cultural perceptions and social interactions.

sublevels.name: Cultural Theory
sublevels.description: Cultural Theory has its roots both in Frankfurt School social theory and the cultural studies program at the University of Birmingham (UK) led by Stuart Hall in the late 20th century. The theoretical/philosophical wing of cultural studies, cultural theory studies media, art, cultural institutions, etc., to develop theories about cultural phenomena, problems, relations, and so on.

sublevels.name: Cultural Evolution
sublevels.description: Cultural evolution is the change over time of non-biological aspects of human society. The process is loosely analogous to biological evolution, although does not necessarily involve Darwinian natural selection, and includes changes in language, art and social behaviour and norms.

sublevels.name: Gender Studies
sublevels.description: Gender studies is an interdisciplinary academic field devoted to analysing gender identity and gendered representation.

sublevels.name: Mens' Studies
sublevels.description: Men's studies is an academic field devoted to topics concerning men, masculinity, gender, culture, politics and sexuality.

sublevels.name: Queer Studies
sublevels.description: Queer studies, sexual diversity studies, or LGBT studies is the study of issues relating to sexual orientation and gender identity usually focusing on lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, gender dysphoria, asexual, queer, questioning, intersex people and cultures.

sublevels.name: Feminism and Feminist Theory
sublevels.description: Feminist theory, also known as feminism, is the belief in the full economic, political, and social equality of the genders.

sublevels.name: Space and Place in Culture
sublevels.description: Space is location, physical space and physical geography, and place is what gives a space meaning, “personality” and a connection to a cultural or personal identity. It is the culturally ascribed meaning given to a space.

sublevels.name: Memory Studies
sublevels.description: Memory Studies examines the social, cultural, cognitive, political and technological shifts affecting how, what and why individuals, groups and societies remember, and forget.

sublevels.name: Regional Cultural Studies
sublevels.description: Academic studies that focus on the culture of a specific geographical region.

sublevels.name: Diaspora Studies
sublevels.description: Diaspora studies is an academic field that studies dispersed ethnic populations, which are often termed diaspora peoples. It specifically looks at the culture of these peoples.

sublevels.name: African American Culture
sublevels.description: African American culture is a subset of American culture, including literature, art, agricultural skills, cuisine, clothing styles, music and language specific to people with partial or total ancestry from Africa.

sublevels.name: African Culture
sublevels.description: The diverse culture of people from Africa, including music, language, art, food, religion, art and literature.

sublevels.name: American Culture
sublevels.description: American Culture is formed of European American, Asian American, African American, Latin American, and Native American peoples and their cultures. The United States has its own distinct social and cultural characteristics, such as dialect, music, arts, social habits, cuisine, and folklore.

sublevels.name: Asian Culture
sublevels.description: Asian culture encompasses the collective and diverse customs and traditions of art, architecture, music, literature, lifestyle, philosophy, politics and religion that have been practiced and maintained by the numerous ethnic groups of the continent of Asia.

sublevels.name: Australasian Culture
sublevels.description: Australasian Culture encompasses the collective and diverse customs and traditions of art, architecture, music, literature, lifestyle, philosophy, politics and religion that have been practiced and maintained by the numerous ethnic groups of the continent of Australia, New Zealand, New Guinea, and the neighbouring islands of the Pacific.

sublevels.name: British Culture
sublevels.description: The culture of Great Britain and the individual nations, England, Wales, Scotland, and Northern Ireland, which primarily includes literature and sport, along with film, television, food, and theatre.

sublevels.name: European Culture
sublevels.description: The study of European culture - art, literature, history, film, philosophy, music, and architecture.

sublevels.name: Latin American Culture
sublevels.description: Latin American culture is culture of the people of Latin America and includes literature, high art, popular culture, music, folk art, and dance, as well as religion and other customary practices.

sublevels.name: Latino Culture
sublevels.description: Latino culture is an academic discipline which studies the culture of people born in Latin America and living in the United States.

sublevels.name: Middle Eastern Culture
sublevels.description: Studying the different cultural traditions and aspects of Middle Eastern and Arab countries.

sublevels.name: Global and International Culture
sublevels.description: Global culture is a set of shared experiences, norms, symbols and ideas that unite people at the global level.

sublevels.name: Linguistics
sublevels.description: Linguistics is the scientific study of language including the study of grammar, syntax, and phonetics. Specific branches of linguistics include sociolinguistics, dialectology, psycholinguistics, computational linguistics, comparative linguistics, and structural linguistics.

sublevels.name: Applied Linguistics
sublevels.description: Applied linguistics is an interdisciplinary field which identifies, investigates, and offers solutions to language-related real-life problems. It the branch of linguistics concerned with practical applications of language studies, for example language teaching, translation, and speech therapy.

sublevels.name: Language Policy and Planning
sublevels.description: Language policy and planning refers to the deliberate efforts made by governments, institutions, and communities to manage and regulate the use of languages within a particular jurisdiction or social context. It involves making decisions about language-related issues such as language choice, language education, language rights, language maintenance, and language revitalization. Language policy and planning are crucial for promoting linguistic diversity, ensuring effective communication, and addressing social, cultural, and political concerns related to language use.

sublevels.name: Linguistic Anthropology
sublevels.description: Linguistic anthropology is a branch of anthropology that studies the role of language in the social lives of individuals and communities. Linguistic anthropology explores how language shapes communication. Linguistic anthropologists have ventured into the study of everyday encounters, language socialization, ritual and political events, scientific discourse, verbal art, language contact and language shift, literacy events, and media.

sublevels.name: Language Translation
sublevels.description: Language translation refers to the process of converting written or spoken content from one language into another while preserving its meaning and intent. some key aspects related to language translation are Translation Process, Translation Techniques, Translation Tools, Specialized Translation, Interpretation, Machine Translation.

sublevels.name: Sociolinguistics
sublevels.description: It examines the relationship between language and society. It explores how language varies and changes within social groups, communities, and different cultural contexts. Sociolinguistics investigates the social, cultural, and political factors that influence language use, attitudes, and variation.

sublevels.name: Research Methods in Language and Linguistics
sublevels.description: The systematic approaches and techniques used to investigate and analyze language-related phenomena. These methods allow researchers to collect data, analyze it, draw conclusions, and contribute to the understanding of language structure, usage, acquisition, and processing.

sublevels.name: Discourse Analysis
sublevels.description: Discourse analysis is the research approach within the field of linguistics that focuses on the study of language in use, particularly how language is used to construct meaning, represent social interactions, and shape social reality. It involves the systematic analysis of spoken or written language data to uncover underlying linguistic patterns, textual structures, textual organization, pragmatic features and functions of discourse.

sublevels.name: Intercultural Communication
sublevels.description: Intercultural Communication is the ability to understand the differences in how people from a variety of cultures act, communicate, and perceive the world around them

sublevels.name: Computational Linguistics
sublevels.description: Computational linguistics is an interdisciplinary field concerned with the computational modelling of natural language, as well as the study of appropriate computational approaches to linguistic questions. In general, computational linguistics draws upon linguistics, computer science, artificial intelligence, math, logic, philosophy, cognitive science, cognitive psychology, psycholinguistics, anthropology and neuroscience, among others.

sublevels.name: Machine Translation
sublevels.description: Machine translation refers to the automated process of translating text or speech from one language to another using computer algorithms and models. It aims to enable communication and understanding between people who speak different languages.

sublevels.name: Multilingualism
sublevels.description: The ability to speak and understand multiple languages.  Multilingualism can exist at individual, societal, or global levels and offers numerous benefits and opportunities.

sublevels.name: Bilingualism
sublevels.description: The ability to speak and understand two languages fluently. Bilingual individuals are proficient in two languages and can effectively communicate, comprehend, read, and write in both languages.

sublevels.name: International and Intercultural Communication
sublevels.description: Intercultural communication refers to how communication behavior is affected when people from different cultures interact and differ in how they perceive the world around them. One way to understand intercultural communication is to see it as communication that unfolds in symbolic intercultural spaces.

sublevels.name: Language Teaching and Learning
sublevels.description: Language teaching and learning refers to the processes and practices involved in acquiring, teaching, and mastering a particular language. It encompasses various approaches, methods, and techniques used to facilitate language acquisition and proficiency development. Language teaching and learning can occur in formal educational settings, language schools, etc.

sublevels.name: Psycholinguistics and Cognitive Linguistics
sublevels.description: Psycholinguistics and Cognitive Linguistics investigates the psychological processes involved in the use of language and the influence of language in our cognitive interaction with the world. It includes language comprehension, language production, and first and second language acquisition as well as linguistic analysis and the perspectival nature of meaning.

sublevels.name: Language Acquisition and Development
sublevels.description: Language acquisition is the ability to understand a language, using it to communicate with others.   Language acquisition and language development can be understood as synonymous

sublevels.name: Languages
sublevels.description: Language is a means of communicating complex ideas or feelings. Although human language can be verbal or non-verbal, it is more complex than any form of animal communication and reflects the culture of its speakers.

sublevels.name: Germanic Languages
sublevels.description: Germanic languages refer to a branch of the Indo-European language family that includes various languages spoken primarily in Europe. The Germanic language family is divided into three main groups: West Germanic, North Germanic, and East Germanic.

sublevels.name: Oriental or Semitic Languages
sublevels.description: Oriental Languages are a group of languages primarily spoken in East Asia. This category includes languages such as Chinese (Mandarin, Cantonese, etc.), Japanese, Korean, Vietnamese, Thai, Burmese, and many others. These languages are linguistically diverse and have distinct grammatical structures, writing systems, and phonetic features. Semitic languages are a branch of the Afro-Asiatic language family and are primarily spoken in the Middle East and parts of North Africa. languages include Arabic (the most widely spoken Semitic language), Hebrew, Amharic (spoken in Ethiopia), Aramaic, and others.

sublevels.name: Asian Languages
sublevels.description: The languages spoken across the vast and diverse continent of Asia. examples such as Mandarin Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Hindi, Bengali

sublevels.name: Ameri-Indian Languages
sublevels.description: Ameri-Indian languages, also known as Native American languages or Indigenous languages of the Americas, refer to the diverse array of languages spoken by Indigenous peoples in the Americas before the arrival of European colonizers. examples such as Navajo, Cherokee, Quechua, Ojibwe, Mohawk, Nahuatl, Aymara.

sublevels.name: Sign Languages
sublevels.description: Sign languages are visual-gestural languages used primarily by deaf and hard-of-hearing individuals to communicate. They are distinct languages with their own grammar, vocabulary, and syntax, separate from spoken languages. few examples of sign languages American Sign Language (ASL), British Sign Language (BSL), French Sign Language (LSF), Japanese Sign Language (JSL), Auslan.

sublevels.name: African Languages
sublevels.description: The diverse range of languages spoken across the African continent. Africa is incredibly linguistically diverse, with over 2,000 distinct languages belonging to different language families. These languages play a crucial role in expressing cultural identities, preserving heritage, and facilitating communication within communities. such as Swahili, Amharic,  Yoruba, Zulu, Hausa, Wolof, etc.

sublevels.name: Finno-Ugric Languages
sublevels.description: Finno-Ugric languages refer to a language family that includes the languages spoken by the Finno-Ugric peoples in Northern Europe and Western Siberia. This language family is a subgroup of the larger Uralic language family, which also includes the Samoyedic languages.

sublevels.name: Romance Languages
sublevels.description: Romance languages are a group of languages derived from Latin, which was spoken by the Romans during the Roman Empire. These languages are primarily spoken in Western Europe, Latin America, and various other regions influenced by Romance-speaking populations. The term "Romance" originates from the Latin word "Romanicus," meaning "in the Roman manner."

sublevels.name: Greek
sublevels.description: Greek refers to the language spoken primarily in Greece and Cyprus. It is one of the oldest recorded languages in the world and has a rich history and cultural significance. Greek is an Indo-European language, specifically belonging to the Hellenic branch, and it has influenced many other languages throughout history.

sublevels.name: Slavic and Baltic Languages
sublevels.description: Slavic languages belong to the Indo-European language family and are primarily spoken in Eastern Europe, as well as parts of Central Europe and the Balkans. They are further divided into three main branches: West Slavic, East Slavic, and South Slavic. while Baltic languages are also part of the Indo-European language family and are spoken in the Baltic region of Northeastern Europe, primarily in Latvia and Lithuania. The two main Baltic languages are Lithuanian and Latvian.

sublevels.name: Celtic
sublevels.description: Celtic refers to a group of related languages and cultures that were historically spoken by Celtic peoples across parts of Western Europe. The Celtic language family is divided into two main branches: Continental Celtic and Insular Celtic.

sublevels.name: Uralic-Altaic Languages
sublevels.description: The classification of Uralic-Altaic as a language family combining Uralic and Altaic languages is a matter of debate among linguists. The Altaic language family hypothesis suggests a connection between the Turkic, Mongolic, and Tungusic languages, while the Uralic language family includes languages such as Finnish, Hungarian, Estonian, and others.

sublevels.name: Philology
sublevels.description: Philology is an interdisciplinary field of study that encompasses the historical, comparative, and critical analysis of languages and literature. It involves the study of texts, their historical context, linguistic evolution, and cultural significance. The term "philology" derives from the Greek words "philos" (love) and "logos" (word, study). Philology traditionally involves the study of ancient and classical languages, such as Latin and Ancient Greek, as well as the analysis of historical texts and their interpretation.

sublevels.name: Stylistics
sublevels.description: Stylistics is a branch of linguistics and literary analysis that focuses on the study of style in language and literature. It explores how linguistic choices, such as vocabulary, syntax, and figurative language, contribute to the overall meaning and impact of a text. Stylistics examines the way language is used to convey meaning beyond the literal level.

sublevels.name: Theoretical Linguistics
sublevels.description: Theoretical linguistics is a term in linguistics which, like the related term general linguistics, can be understood in different ways. Both can be taken as a reference to theory of language, or the branch of linguistics which inquires into the nature of language and seeks to answer fundamental questions as to what language is, or what the common ground of all languages is. The goal of theoretical linguistics can also be the construction of a general theoretical framework for the description of language.

sublevels.name: Semiotics
sublevels.description: Semiotics (also called semiotic studies) is the systematic study of sign processes (semiosis) and meaning making. Semiosis is any activity, conduct, or process that involves signs, where a sign is defined as anything that communicates something, usually called a meaning, to the sign's interpreter.

sublevels.name: Comparative Linguistics
sublevels.description: Comparative linguistics, or comparative-historical linguistics (formerly comparative philology) is a branch of historical linguistics that is concerned with comparing languages to establish their historical relatedness.

sublevels.name: Lexicology / Vocabulary
sublevels.description: Lexicology is the branch of linguistics that analyzes the lexicon of a specific language. A word is the smallest meaningful unit of a language that can stand on its own, and is made up of small components called morphemes and even smaller elements known as phonemes, or distinguishing sounds. Lexicology examines every feature of a word – including formation, spelling, origin, usage, and definition.

sublevels.name: Phonology and Phonetics
sublevels.description: Phonetics deals with the production of speech sounds by humans, often without prior knowledge of the language being spoken. Phonology is about patterns of sounds, especially different patterns of sounds in different languages, or within each language, different patterns of sounds in different positions in words etc.

sublevels.name: Pragmatics
sublevels.description: In linguistics and related fields, pragmatics is the study of how context contributes to meaning. The field of study evaluates how human language is utilized in social interactions, as well as the relationship between the interpreter and the interpreted.

sublevels.name: Orthography
sublevels.description: An orthography is a set of conventions for writing a language, including norms of spelling, hyphenation, capitalization, word boundaries, emphasis, and punctuation.

sublevels.name: Graphemics
sublevels.description: Graphemics or graphematics is the linguistic study of writing systems and their basic components, i.e. graphemes.

sublevels.name: Grammar
sublevels.description: Grammar is the systematic study and set of rules that govern the structure of language, including the formation of words, phrases, and sentences. It encompasses the principles that dictate syntax, morphology, and phonology, enabling clear and meaningful communication.

sublevels.name: Semantics
sublevels.description: Semantics is the study of reference, meaning, or truth.

sublevels.name: Historical Linguistics
sublevels.description: The study of language change over time. It investigates how languages evolve, reconstructs earlier stages of languages, and explores the relationships between different languages and language families. Historical linguistics aims to understand the processes and mechanisms of language change and the historical developments that have shaped present-day languages.

sublevels.name: Language History
sublevels.description: Language history refers to the study of the development and evolution of languages over time. It involves tracing the origins, changes, and relationships between different languages and language families, as well as understanding the socio-cultural and historical contexts in which these languages have emerged and evolved. Language History, has a broader scope and encompasses the historical, cultural, and social aspects of language use and development as compared to Historical Linguistics

sublevels.name: Classical Linguistics
sublevels.description: covers old Greek/Latin/other languages (Yoka). The classical languages of ancient civilizations, such as Latin and Ancient Greek. It focuses on the analysis, grammar, and interpretation of these classical languages, as well as their historical development and cultural contexts. Classical linguistics explores the structure, syntax, morphology, phonetics, and semantics of classical languages and examines their influence on subsequent languages and literatures.

sublevels.name: Language Change
sublevels.description: The process by which languages undergo modifications, transformations, and developments over time. It is a natural and ongoing phenomenon that occurs at various levels of language, including phonetics, phonology, morphology, syntax, semantics, and lexicon. Language change can occur through a variety of mechanisms and influences, shaping the linguistic systems of a language and reflecting cultural, social, and historical factors.

sublevels.name: Law
sublevels.description: Law is a set of rules that are created and are enforceable by social or governmental institutions to regulate behavior, with its precise definition a matter of longstanding debate. It has been variously described as a science and as the art of justice.

sublevels.name: European Law
sublevels.description: The European Union is based on the rule of law. This means that every action taken by the EU is founded on treaties that have been approved democratically by its members. EU laws help to achieve the objectives of the EU treaties and put EU policies into practice.

sublevels.name: European Fundamental Rights and Freedoms
sublevels.description: The Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union sets out all the personal, civic, political, economic and social rights enjoyed by people in the European Union. The Charter complements national systems but does not replace them.

sublevels.name: European Economic Law
sublevels.description: European Economic Law (EEL) is an internationally renowned programme which over the course of its 20 years of existence has developed a distinctive profile with a blend of competition law, financial law and social law.

sublevels.name: European Criminal Law
sublevels.description: European criminal law is explained as a multi-level field of law, in which the European Union has a normative influence on all criminal proceedings, but also on aspects of substantive criminal law and on the co-operation between Member States.

sublevels.name: Public International Law
sublevels.description: Public International Law governs the legal relationships between sovereign states and other international actors, covering areas such as human rights, international treaties, and conflict resolution.

sublevels.name: Sources and Subjects of International Law, International Organizations
sublevels.description: Sources and Subjects of International Law, International Organizations study the origins, principles, and entities governed by international law, including states, international organizations, and non-state actors.

sublevels.name: Law of the Sea, Air and Outer Space
sublevels.description: The seas, the air and space states have managed to appropriate some zones over which they exercise exclusive, or functional, jurisdiction.

sublevels.name: International Humanitarian Law, Law of Armed Conflict
sublevels.description: International humanitarian law is a set of rules that seek to limit the effects of armed conflict. It protects people who are not or are no longer participating in hostilities and restricts the means and methods of warfare.

sublevels.name: International Economic Law, Trade Law
sublevels.description: International Economic Law, Trade Law encompasses the legal frameworks and regulations governing international economic relations, including trade agreements, investment treaties, and dispute resolution mechanisms.

sublevels.name: International Criminal Law
sublevels.description: International criminal law is a body of public international law designed to prohibit certain categories of conduct commonly viewed as serious atrocities and to make perpetrators of such conduct criminally accountable for their perpetration.

sublevels.name: Human Rights
sublevels.description: Human rights are rights inherent to all human beings, regardless of race, sex, nationality, ethnicity, language, religion, or any other status. Human rights include the right to life and liberty, freedom from slavery and torture, freedom of opinion and expression, the right to work and education, and many more.

sublevels.name: International Environmental Law
sublevels.description: International environmental law is the set of agreements and principles that reflect the world's collective effort to manage our transition to the Anthropocene by resolving our most serious environmental problems, including climate change, ozone depletion and mass extinction of wildlife.

sublevels.name: Public Law
sublevels.description: Public law is the part of law that governs relations between legal persons and a government, between different institutions within a state, between different branches of governments, as well as relationships between persons that are of direct concern to society.

sublevels.name: Fiscal Law
sublevels.description: Fiscal Law relates to public financial resources, government expenditures, revenues, debt or taxation.  Main target groups: officials in tax legislation, administration and tax policy, professionals in financial institutions

sublevels.name: Administrative Law
sublevels.description: Administrative law, the legal framework within which public administration is carried out. It derives from the need to create and develop a system of public administration under law, a concept that may be compared with the much older notion of justice under law.

sublevels.name: Constitutional Law
sublevels.description: Constitutional law deals with the fundamental principles by which the government exercises its authority.

sublevels.name: Financial Law
sublevels.description: Financial law is a field of study and practice that encompasses the laws and regulations governing financial transactions and institutions. It includes a wide range of legal topics, such as banking law, securities regulation, insurance law, and tax law. In research, financial law involves the study and development of legal theories and principles to improve the regulation and practice of financial activities. The field of financial law research covers a wide range of topics, including the impact of financial regulations on the stability and efficiency of financial markets, the development of new legal frameworks for emerging financial practices, and the role of international financial law in regulating cross-border transactions. Banking law refers to the laws and regulations governing the operation of banks and other financial institutions, such as deposit insurance, lending practices, and consumer protection. Securities regulation refers to the laws and regulations governing the issuance, trading, and reporting of securities, such as stocks, bonds, and mutual funds. Insurance law governs the regulation and supervision of insurance companies and the protection of policyholders. Tax law refers to the laws and regulations governing the assessment and collection of taxes, such as income tax, corporate tax, and value-added tax (VAT). Financial law also encompasses international financial law, which deals with the regulation of cross-border financial transactions and the resolution of international financial disputes. In practice, financial law involves the application of legal principles and regulations to financial transactions and institutions, such as the formation and operation of banks and financial companies, the issuance and trading of securities, and the taxation of financial transactions. Financial law also involves the compliance with legal and regulatory requirements, such as anti-money laundering laws, securities disclosure requirements, and tax reporting obligations. Financial law is essential for the proper functioning of financial markets and the economy as a whole. By providing a legal framework for financial transactions and institutions, it helps to ensure the stability, efficiency, and integrity of financial systems, protect the interests of investors and consumers, and promote economic growth and development.

sublevels.name: Fundamentals of Law
sublevels.description: Fundamentals of Law is a basic law that is either a codified constitution, or in countries with uncodified constitutions, a law given to have constitution powers and effect.

sublevels.name: Civil Law
sublevels.description: Civil Law is a legal system based on written codes and statutes, governing private rights and disputes between individuals, including areas such as contracts, property, and family law.

sublevels.name: Common Company Law
sublevels.description: In Common Company Law, whilst a shareholder is often colloquially referred to as the owner of the company - it is clear that the shareholder is not an owner of the company but makes the shareholder a member of the company and entitles them to enforce the provisions of the company's constitution against the company and against other members.

sublevels.name: Common Property and Land Law
sublevels.description: Common law property is a system that most states use to determine the ownership of property. Land law is the form of law that deals with the rights to use, alienate, or exclude others from land. In many jurisdictions, these kinds of property are referred to as real estate or real property, as distinct from personal property.

sublevels.name: Labour Law/Social Law
sublevels.description: Labour Law/Social Law is the Establishment of all kinds of justice for the working people – social, economic, and political.

sublevels.name: Commercial Law
sublevels.description: Commercial law, also known as mercantile law or trade law, is the body of law that applies to the rights, relations, and conduct of persons and business engaged in commerce, merchandising, trade, and sales.

sublevels.name: Common Tort Law
sublevels.description: Common Tort Law deals with and offers remedies for non?contractual civil wrongdoings. A person who experiences legal harm may be able to use tort law to pursue restitution from those who are held accountable or legally liable.

sublevels.name: Civil Procedure Law
sublevels.description: Civil procedure is the body of law that sets out the rules and standards that courts follow when adjudicating civil lawsuits (as opposed to procedures in criminal law matters).

sublevels.name: Equity and Trust in Common Law
sublevels.description: An equitable right is a legal right guaranteed by equity as opposed to a legal right which derives authority from a legal source. Trust law concerns the protection of assets, usually when they are held by one party for another's benefit.

sublevels.name: Family Law
sublevels.description: Family law (also called matrimonial law or the law of domestic relations) is an area of the law that deals with family matters and domestic relations.

sublevels.name: Common Contract Law
sublevels.description: In common law jurisdictions, the formation of a contract generally requires an offer, acceptance, consideration, and mutual intent to be bound. Examples of standard form contracts can include: employment contracts. lease agreements. insurance agreements.

sublevels.name: Environmental Law
sublevels.description: Environmental law refers to a system of legal principles, regulations, and statutes that aim to protect and manage the natural environment and address environmental issues. It encompasses a wide range of legal frameworks at international, national, regional, and local levels, governing various aspects of environmental protection, conservation, and sustainable development. Environmental law encompasses both public and private law and involves the interaction between legal, social, economic, and scientific considerations.

sublevels.name: International Environmental Law
sublevels.description: International environmental law is the set of agreements and principles that reflect the world's collective effort to manage our transition to the Anthropocene by resolving our most serious environmental problems, including climate change, ozone depletion and mass extinction of wildlife.

sublevels.name: IT Law, Media Law, Intellectual Property
sublevels.description: Intellectual property (IP), such as patents, provides legal rights to the exclusive use of the output of creative efforts. For example, a patent on a drug could provide its owner with the right to exclusively market that drug for a defined period of time in exchange for detailed public disclosure of the drug’s characteristics, such as chemical structure.

sublevels.name: Private International Law, International and Foreign Law, Comparative Law
sublevels.description: Private International Law describes the body of law surrounding which law governs when there is a conflict between citizens of different countries. International Law and Foreign Law are two different things.  Foreign Law applies to a single nation, while International Law covers multiple nations and is based on treaties, etc.

sublevels.name: International Sports Law
sublevels.description: International sports law (ISL) can be defined as the set of principles, rules, and processes that guarantee, relating to Sports and to ensure that these laws run smoothly to maintain the sports industry.

sublevels.name: Theories of Law, Philosophy of Law, Legal History
sublevels.description: Philosophy of law (or legal philosophy) is concerned with providing a general philosophical analysis of law and legal institutions. Legal history or the history of law is the study of how law has evolved and why it has changed. Legal history is closely connected to the development of civilisations and operates in the wider context of social history.

sublevels.name: Philosophy of Law
sublevels.description: Philosophy of law is a branch of philosophy that examines the nature of law and law's relationship to other systems of norms, especially ethics and political philosophy.

sublevels.name: Medical Law
sublevels.description: Medical law refers to a branch of law that deals with the legal and ethical issues related to the medical profession, including the rights and duties of healthcare providers, patients, and third-party payers.

sublevels.name: Dispute Resolution, Mediation, Arbitration
sublevels.description: Dispute resolution or dispute settlement is the process of resolving disputes between parties. The term dispute resolution is sometimes used interchangeably with conflict resolution.  In a mediation process, a neutral, trained mediator works to help disputants come to a consensus on their own. In arbitration, a neutral, trained arbitrator serves as a judge who is responsible for resolving the dispute.

sublevels.name: Criminal Law and Criminal Procedure Law
sublevels.description: Criminal law generally defines the rights and obligations of individuals in society. Some common issues in criminal law are the elements of specific crimes and the elements of various criminal defenses. Criminal procedure generally concerns the enforcement of individuals' rights during the criminal process.

sublevels.name: Education
sublevels.description: Education is an act or process of imparting or acquiring general knowledge, developing the powers of reasoning and judgment, and generally of preparing oneself or others intellectually for mature life. OR The act or process of imparting or acquiring particular knowledge or skills, as for a profession.

sublevels.name: Inclusive Education
sublevels.description: Inclusive education means all children in the same classrooms, in the same schools. It means real learning opportunities for groups who have traditionally been excluded – not only children with disabilities, but speakers of minority languages too.

sublevels.name: Disability Pedagogy
sublevels.description: Disability Pedagogy is the study and practice of inclusive teaching approaches that recognize disability as a form of human diversity, aiming to remove barriers and promote equitable learning for all students.

sublevels.name: Special and Gifted Education
sublevels.description: Gifted education (also known as gifted and talented education (GATE), talented and gifted programs (TAG), or G&T education) is a sort of education used for children who have been identified as gifted and talented.  The main approaches to gifted education are enrichment and acceleration. An enrichment program teaches additional, deeper material, but keeps the student progressing through the curriculum at the same rate as other students.  Special education (known as special-needs education, aided education, exceptional education, alternative provision, exceptional student education, special ed., SDC, or SPED) is the practice of educating students in a way that accommodates their individual differences, disabilities, and special needs. This involves the individually planned and systematically monitored arrangement of teaching procedures, adapted equipment and materials, and accessible settings. These interventions are designed to help individuals with special needs achieve a higher level of personal self-sufficiency and success in school and in their community, which may not be available if the student were only given access to a typical classroom education.

sublevels.name: School and Schooling
sublevels.description: A school is an educational institution designed to provide learning spaces and learning environments for the teaching of students under the direction of teachers. Most countries have systems of formal education, which is sometimes compulsory. In these systems, students progress through a series of schools. Schooling refers to the process of attending school and learning the body of knowledge taught in a curriculum.

sublevels.name: Educational Research
sublevels.description: Educational research refers to the systematic study and investigation of educational topics, issues, and phenomena. It is a field of inquiry that aims to generate new knowledge, advance understanding, and improve educational practices and policies. Educational research encompasses a wide range of methodologies, approaches, and areas of study, addressing various aspects of teaching, learning, curriculum, assessment, and educational systems.

sublevels.name: Sport Education and Didactics
sublevels.description: Sport Education is a curriculum and instruction model designed for delivery within physical education. Modifications can be made to suit each age category, activity or setting. It is most effective with games based activities and with participants who have a good base level of competence. Didactics refers to the science of teaching and instruction for any given field of study. Based on theoretical foundations, a didactic approach involves a very structured and informed approach to teaching and instruction.

sublevels.name: Outdoor Education
sublevels.description: Outdoor Education is an experiential learning approach that uses outdoor and natural settings to facilitate personal and social development, environmental awareness, and the acquisition of technical and practical skills. This field explores the theory, methods, and evaluation of outdoor education programs, as well as their role in fostering holistic and lifelong learning.

sublevels.name: Mathematics Education
sublevels.description: In contemporary education, mathematics education—known in Europe as the didactics or pedagogy of mathematics—is the practice of teaching, learning, and carrying out scholarly research into the transfer of mathematical knowledge.  Although research into mathematics education is primarily concerned with the tools, methods, and approaches that facilitate practice or the study of practice, it also covers an extensive field of study encompassing a variety of different concepts, theories and methods. National and international organisations regularly hold conferences and publish literature in order to improve mathematics education.

sublevels.name: Skills
sublevels.description: A skill is the learned ability to act with determined results with good execution often within a given amount of time, energy, or both. Skills can often be divided into domain-general and domain-specific skills.

sublevels.name: Thesis and Dissertation
sublevels.description: A thesis, or dissertation is a document submitted in support of candidature for an academic degree or professional qualification presenting the author's research and findings. In some contexts, the word thesis or a cognate is used for part of a bachelor's or master's course, while dissertation is normally applied to a doctorate.

sublevels.name: Study and Learning Skills
sublevels.description: Study and learning skills encompass a range of strategies, techniques, and habits that help individuals effectively acquire, process, retain, and apply knowledge. These skills are essential for successful learning and academic performance. They involve developing effective study habits, time management, critical thinking, note-taking, and information organization.

sublevels.name: Writing Skills
sublevels.description: Writing Skills is the study and practice of effective written communication across various formats and contexts, such as academic, professional, and creative writing. This field emphasizes the development of skills in grammar, syntax, organization, style, and argumentation, as well as the ability to critically reflect on one's own writing and the writing of others.

sublevels.name: Career Skills
sublevels.description: Career skills are the sum of your professional knowledge, skills and experience. They determine how successful you are in making decisions, influencing outcomes, effecting change and doing a good job.

sublevels.name: Revision and Exam
sublevels.description: Revision and exam preparation are essential components of the learning process, particularly in educational systems that utilize formal assessments. Revision typically refers to the process of reviewing and reinforcing previously learned material, such as textbooks, lecture notes, and class activities. Exam preparation focuses specifically on getting ready for upcoming assessments.

sublevels.name: Critical Thinking
sublevels.description: Critical thinking is the intellectually disciplined process of actively and skillfully conceptualizing, applying, analyzing, synthesizing, and/or evaluating information gathered from, or generated by, observation, experience, reflection, reasoning, or communication, as a guide to belief and action.

sublevels.name: Life Skills
sublevels.description: Life skills are abilities for adaptive and positive behavior that enable humans to deal effectively with the demands and challenges of life. Life Skills are a group of psychosocial competencies and interpersonal skills that help people make informed decisions, solve problems, think critically and creatively, communicate effectively, build healthy relationships, empathize with others, and cope with and manage their lives in a healthy and productive manner.

sublevels.name: Organization and Leadership
sublevels.description: Organizational leadership is a management approach in which leaders help set strategic goals for the organization while motivating individuals within the group to successfully carry out assignments in service to those goals.

sublevels.name: Research Skills
sublevels.description: Research skills refer to the ability to search for, locate, extract, organise, evaluate and use or present information that is relevant to a particular topic.

sublevels.name: Groupwork and Presentation
sublevels.description: Groupwork and Presentation is to work together to have ONE introduction, body, and conclusion for the presentation. One person compiles the slides from everyone into one slideshow. Use only one template/slide style for the entire presentation. Everyone works on their slides and sends/gives them to the one compiling.

sublevels.name: Studying Abroad
sublevels.description: Studying abroad means taking classes at a university in a different country for academic credit that will count towards degree.

sublevels.name: Literacy
sublevels.description: Literacy in its broadest sense describes "particular ways of thinking about and doing reading and writing" with the purpose of understanding or expressing thoughts or ideas in written form in some specific context of use.

sublevels.name: Educational Philosophy
sublevels.description: An education philosophy is a set of educational beliefs and core values of a person and/or organisation. It directs the purposes and objectives of educational planning, programs and processes. It focuses on what is the purpose of education, what should be taught, and how it should be taught. In contrast, the philosophy of education is the branch of applied philosophy that investigates the nature of education as well as its aims and problems.

sublevels.name: Holistic Education
sublevels.description: Holistic education is an approach to learning that considers the whole person, focusing on the development of individuals intellectually, emotionally, socially, physically, and spiritually. It aims to cultivate well-rounded individuals who can thrive in various aspects of life and contribute positively to society. Holistic education goes beyond the traditional emphasis on academic achievement and incorporates a broader range of skills, values, and qualities.

sublevels.name: Science Education
sublevels.description: Science education is the teaching and learning of science to school children, college students, or adults within the general public. The field of science education includes work in science content, science process (the scientific method), some social science, and some teaching pedagogy.

sublevels.name: Education in Physics
sublevels.description: Physics education refers to the methods currently used to teach physics. Physics Education Research refers to an area of pedagogical research that seeks to improve those methods.

sublevels.name: Research Skills
sublevels.description: Research skills refer to the ability to search for, locate, extract, organise, evaluate and use or present information that is relevant to a particular topic.

sublevels.name: Technology and Design education
sublevels.description: Technology and Design Education is the study of teaching approaches and curriculum development with regards to the intersections of technology, engineering, and design, aiming to equip students with critical thinking, problem-solving, and technical skills.

sublevels.name: Mathematics Education
sublevels.description: In contemporary education, mathematics education—known in Europe as the didactics or pedagogy of mathematics—is the practice of teaching, learning, and carrying out scholarly research into the transfer of mathematical knowledge.  Although research into mathematics education is primarily concerned with the tools, methods, and approaches that facilitate practice or the study of practice, it also covers an extensive field of study encompassing a variety of different concepts, theories and methods. National and international organisations regularly hold conferences and publish literature in order to improve mathematics education.

sublevels.name: Outdoor Education
sublevels.description: Outdoor Education is an experiential learning approach that uses outdoor and natural settings to facilitate personal and social development, environmental awareness, and the acquisition of technical and practical skills. This field explores the theory, methods, and evaluation of outdoor education programs, as well as their role in fostering holistic and lifelong learning.

sublevels.name: Chemistry Education
sublevels.description: Chemistry education (or chemical education) is the study of teaching and learning chemistry. It is one subset of STEM education or discipline-based education research (DBER).

sublevels.name: Alternative Education
sublevels.description: Alternative education refers to educational approaches, environments, or programs that diverge from mainstream schooling in terms of curriculum, structure, instructional methods, or underlying values and philosophies, often emphasizing individualized learning, inclusivity, and progressive pedagogy.

sublevels.name: Experiential Education
sublevels.description: Experiential education is an approach to learning that emphasizes direct engagement with real-world experiences as a means of acquiring knowledge, skills, and attitudes. It involves active participation, reflection, and application of learning in practical contexts, going beyond traditional classroom-based instruction.

sublevels.name: Holistic Education
sublevels.description: Holistic education is an approach to learning that considers the whole person, focusing on the development of individuals intellectually, emotionally, socially, physically, and spiritually. It aims to cultivate well-rounded individuals who can thrive in various aspects of life and contribute positively to society. Holistic education goes beyond the traditional emphasis on academic achievement and incorporates a broader range of skills, values, and qualities.

sublevels.name: Outdoor Education
sublevels.description: Outdoor Education is an experiential learning approach that uses outdoor and natural settings to facilitate personal and social development, environmental awareness, and the acquisition of technical and practical skills. This field explores the theory, methods, and evaluation of outdoor education programs, as well as their role in fostering holistic and lifelong learning.

sublevels.name: Higher Education
sublevels.description: Higher education is tertiary education leading to the award of an academic degree. Higher education, which makes up a component of post-secondary, third-level, or tertiary education, is an optional final stage of formal learning that occurs after completion of secondary education. It represents levels 5, 6, 7, and 8 of the 2011 version of the International Standard Classification of Education structure. Tertiary education at a nondegree level is sometimes referred to as further education or continuing education as distinct from higher education.

sublevels.name: Technical and Vocational Education and Training
sublevels.description: Vocational education is education that prepares people to a skilled craft as an artisan, trade as a tradesperson, or work as a technician. Vocational Education can also be seen as that type of education given to an individual to prepare that individual to be gainfully employed or self employed with requisite skill. Profession requires training and qualification whereas vocation is the innate ability in an individual towards a particular occupation. In modern times, a vocation refers to an occupation for which a person has special abilities or is trained to do that job.

sublevels.name: Engineering and Technology Education
sublevels.description: Engineering education is the activity of teaching knowledge and principles to the professional practice of engineering. It includes an initial education (bachelor's and/or master's degree), and any advanced education and specializations that follow. Engineering education is typically accompanied by additional postgraduate examinations and supervised training as the requirements for a professional engineering license. The length of education, and training to qualify as a basic professional engineer, is typically 5 years, with 15–20 years for an engineer who takes responsibility for major projects.  Technology education is the study of technology, in which students "learn about the processes and knowledge related to technology". As a field of study, it covers the human's ability to shape and change the physical world to meet needs, by manipulating materials and tools with techniques. It addresses the disconnect between wide usage and the lack of knowledge about technical components of technologies used and how to fix them.

sublevels.name: Medical Education
sublevels.description: Medical education is education related to the practice of being a medical practitioner, including the initial training to become a physician (i.e., medical school and internship) and additional training thereafter (e.g., residency, fellowship, and continuing medical education).  Medical education and training varies considerably across the world. Various teaching methodologies have been used in medical education, which is an active area of educational research.

sublevels.name: Teaching and Teacher Education
sublevels.description: Teaching is the practice implemented by a teacher aimed at transmitting skills (knowledge, know-how, and interpersonal skills) to a learner, a student, or any other audience in the context of an educational institution. Teaching is closely related to learning, the student's activity of appropriating this knowledge. Teaching is part of the broader concept of education. Teacher education or teacher training refers to programs, policies, procedures, and provision designed to equip (prospective) teachers with the knowledge, attitudes, behaviors, approaches, methodologies and skills they require to perform their tasks effectively in the classroom, school, and wider community. The professionals who engage in training the prospective teachers are called teacher educators (or, in some contexts, teacher trainers).

sublevels.name: Environmental and Sustainability Education
sublevels.description: Environmental education (EE) refers to organized efforts to teach how natural environments function, and particularly, how human beings can manage behavior and ecosystems to live sustainably. It is a multi-disciplinary field integrating disciplines such as biology, chemistry, physics, ecology, earth science, atmospheric science, mathematics, and geography. Education for Sustainable Development means including key sustainable development issues into teaching and learning; for example, climate change, disaster risk reduction, biodiversity, poverty reduction, and sustainable consumption.

sublevels.name: Outdoor Education
sublevels.description: Outdoor Education is an experiential learning approach that uses outdoor and natural settings to facilitate personal and social development, environmental awareness, and the acquisition of technical and practical skills. This field explores the theory, methods, and evaluation of outdoor education programs, as well as their role in fostering holistic and lifelong learning.

sublevels.name: Lifelong Learning
sublevels.description: Lifelong learning is broadly defined as the ongoing, voluntary, and self-motivated pursuit of knowledge for either personal or professional reasons. It is important for an individual's competitiveness and employability, but also enhances social inclusion, active citizenship, and personal development.

sublevels.name: Personal Development
sublevels.description: Personal development focuses on enhancing one's self-awareness, knowledge, skills, and attitudes with the goal of achieving personal fulfillment and reaching one's potential. It involves a conscious effort to develop and refine aspects of oneself, such as emotional intelligence, self-esteem, resilience, goal-setting, and self-motivation.

sublevels.name: Informal Education
sublevels.description: Informal education is a general term for education that can occur outside of a traditional lecture or school based learning systems. The term even include customized-learning based on individual student interests within a curriculum inside a regular classroom, but is not limited to that setting.

sublevels.name: Adult Education
sublevels.description: Adult education is education aimed at mature students that have already taken part in the workforce. Learning as a mature student gives individuals the chance to gain new skills and expand their knowledge.

sublevels.name: Creative Arts Pedagogy
sublevels.description: Creative arts pedagogy or education is when students are able to use imagination and critical thinking to create new and meaningful forms of ideas where they can take risks, be independent and flexible. Arts in education is an expanding field of educational research and practicehrough arts experiences. In this context, the arts can include performing arts education (dance, drama, music), literature and poetry, storytelling, Visual arts education in film, craft, design, digital arts, media and photography

sublevels.name: History of Education
sublevels.description: The first education system was created in Xia dynasty (2076–1600 BC). During Xia dynasty, government built schools to educate aristocrats about rituals, literature and archery (important for ancient Chinese aristocrats). During Shang dynasty (1600 BC to 1046 BC), normal people (farmers, workers etc.)  Perhaps the earliest formal school was developed in Egypt's Middle Kingdom under the direction of Kheti, treasurer to Mentuhotep II (2061-2010 BC). In Mesopotamia, the early logographic system of cuneiform script took many years to master. Thus only a limited number of individuals were hired as scribes to be trained in its reading and writing. Only royal offspring and sons of the rich and professionals such as scribes, physicians, and temple administrators, were schooled.

sublevels.name: Didactics and Teaching Methodology
sublevels.description: Didactics and teaching methodology are two related concepts in the field of education that focus on the practice of teaching and learning. While they are interconnected, they have distinct meanings. Didactics refers to the science or theory of teaching. It encompasses the principles, methods, and techniques used to facilitate effective teaching and learning processes. Teaching methodology, on the other hand, refers to the specific approaches, techniques, and strategies used by teachers to deliver instruction and facilitate learning.

sublevels.name: Curriculum Studies
sublevels.description: Curriculum studies, also known as curriculum theory or curriculum inquiry, is a field of study within education that focuses on the design, development, implementation, and evaluation of educational curricula. It examines the theoretical and practical aspects of curriculum, including its content, structure, objectives, and methods.

sublevels.name: Assessment and Testing
sublevels.description: Assessment and testing are two related concepts in the field of education that focus on evaluating and measuring students' knowledge, skills, and understanding. Although they are interconnected, they have distinct meanings and purposes. Assessment refers to the ongoing process of gathering evidence and information about students' learning progress, achievements, and areas of growth. Testing, on the other hand, refers to a specific form of assessment that involves measuring students' knowledge and skills through standardized or formalized assessments.

sublevels.name: Language Education
sublevels.description: Language education refers to the field of teaching and learning languages, with a primary focus on developing proficiency in a specific language or languages. It encompasses various approaches, methods, and strategies used to facilitate language acquisition, communication skills, cultural understanding, and language proficiency.

sublevels.name: Media Education
sublevels.description: Media literacy education is the process used to advance media literacy competencies, and it is intended to promote awareness of media influence and create an active stance towards both consuming and creating media.

sublevels.name: Digital Education and Educational Technology
sublevels.description: Digital learning can take form in a blog, a video, a real-time lecture or seminar or even just an audio file. Digital learning will include at least one piece of technology such as a computer, laptop or mobile phone. One important definition of educational technology focuses on “the technological tools and media that assist in the communication of knowledge, and its development and exchange.” Take augmented reality and virtual reality, for example.

sublevels.name: Social Education
sublevels.description: Social education is education for the betterment of the individual's social, economic and political and moral life. Social Education is education which enables a community to assume direction of its own development.

sublevels.name: Education Policy
sublevels.description: Education policy is the study of governmental guidelines and decisions that govern the operation of education systems. This includes both childhood education and adult education.

sublevels.name: Educational Inequality
sublevels.description: Critical Race Theory in Education is an interdisciplinary framework that examines how race and racism influence educational systems, policies, and practices

sublevels.name: Social Work Consulting
sublevels.description: Social work consulting is a field of study that focuses on providing expert guidance, advice, and support to individuals, organizations, and communities in addressing social issues and improving social work practices. Social work consultants apply their knowledge, skills, and experience to offer specialized insights, recommendations, and solutions to enhance the effectiveness and impact of social work interventions and programs.

sublevels.name: Domestic and Sexual Violence
sublevels.description: Domestic and sexual violence is a subfield of social work that focuses on addressing and preventing interpersonal violence within the context of intimate relationships and sexual encounters. It involves providing support, advocacy, and interventions for individuals and communities affected by domestic and sexual violence, as well as working towards creating social change to eliminate such violence.

sublevels.name: Theory and Method in Social Work
sublevels.description: Theory and method in social work refer to the foundational frameworks, concepts, and approaches used to understand and address social issues, as well as the systematic procedures and techniques employed in social work practice. Theories provide the theoretical underpinnings and conceptual frameworks that inform social work interventions, while methods outline the systematic steps and techniques used to implement these interventions and achieve desired outcomes.

sublevels.name: Social Care
sublevels.description: Social care is the provision of services and support to individuals and families to aid their physical, emotional, and social well-being, including child protection, elder care, and assistance for people with disabilities or mental health issues.

sublevels.name: Social Work Education
sublevels.description: Social Work Education involves the academic and practical training of individuals to become professional social workers, focusing on skills, ethics, and knowledge required for social services.

sublevels.name: Children and Youth Work
sublevels.description: Children and Youth Work involves the development and implementation of programs, activities, and services aimed at supporting and enhancing the well-being, education, and personal development of children and young people. This includes working with families, schools, community organizations, and government agencies to address the needs of diverse populations.

sublevels.name: Education Science
sublevels.description: Education sciences, also known as education studies, education theory, and traditionally called pedagogy, seek to describe, understand, and prescribe education policy and practice. Education sciences include many topics, such as pedagogy, andragogy, curriculum, learning, and education policy, organization and leadership. Educational thought is informed by many disciplines, such as history, philosophy, sociology, and psychology.

sublevels.name: Sociology of Education
sublevels.description: The sociology of education is a field of study that examines the social processes, structures, and dynamics within educational institutions and systems. It explores the interactions between education and society, focusing on how education shapes and is shaped by social factors, such as social class, gender, race, ethnicity, and social inequalities.

sublevels.name: International and Comparative Education
sublevels.description: International and comparative education is a field of study that examines educational systems, policies, practices, and outcomes across different countries and regions. It focuses on understanding the similarities, differences, and interconnections between education systems globally, as well as the factors that shape them.

sublevels.name: Research Skills
sublevels.description: Research skills refer to the ability to search for, locate, extract, organise, evaluate and use or present information that is relevant to a particular topic.

sublevels.name: Educational Research
sublevels.description: Educational research refers to the systematic study and investigation of educational topics, issues, and phenomena. It is a field of inquiry that aims to generate new knowledge, advance understanding, and improve educational practices and policies. Educational research encompasses a wide range of methodologies, approaches, and areas of study, addressing various aspects of teaching, learning, curriculum, assessment, and educational systems.

sublevels.name: Pedagogy
sublevels.description: Pedagogy, most commonly understood as the approach to teaching, is the theory and practice of learning, and how this process influences, and is influenced by, the social, political and psychological development of learners. Pedagogy, taken as an academic discipline, is the study of how knowledge and skills are imparted in an educational context, and it considers the interactions that take place during learning. Both the theory and practice of pedagogy vary greatly as they reflect different social, political, and cultural contexts

sublevels.name: Early Childhood Education
sublevels.description: Early childhood education (ECE), also known as nursery education, is a branch of education theory that relates to the teaching of children (formally and informally) from birth up to the age of eight. Traditionally, this is up to the equivalent of third grade. ECE is described as an important period in child development.

sublevels.name: Literacy
sublevels.description: Literacy in its broadest sense describes "particular ways of thinking about and doing reading and writing" with the purpose of understanding or expressing thoughts or ideas in written form in some specific context of use.

sublevels.name: Childhood Education
sublevels.description: Early Childhood Care and Education (ECCE) in the Indian context is generally defined as the care and education of children from birth to eight years. It includes: Early stimulation programmes through crèches/homes stimulation for 0-3 year olds.  Education is the foundation of a child's future well-being. Children's education creates various opportunities to help them live better lives. It can also help shape the society at large. With the right education, a child can help the country develop and progress at a faster pace.

sublevels.name: Urban Education
sublevels.description: Urban education refers to the field of study, practice, and policy focused on the educational needs of students and communities in metropolitan areas, especially inner cities. It involves understanding the unique challenges and opportunities present in these contexts, including issues of diversity, poverty, and access to quality education.

sublevels.name: Rural Education
sublevels.description: Rural education encompasses the schooling provided in areas with low population density, often facing distinct challenges and advantages compared to urban and suburban counterparts.

sublevels.name: Educational Policy and Politics
sublevels.description: Educational policy and politics refer to the processes, decisions, and actions related to the development, implementation, and evaluation of policies that shape the educational system. It involves the intersection of educational goals, societal needs, political agendas, and the allocation of resources. Educational policy and politics influence various aspects of education, including curriculum, funding, assessment, teacher training, school governance, and educational equity.

sublevels.name: Creativity Studies
sublevels.description: Creativity Studies is a discipline that studies the psychological, sociocultural, systemic, and distributed understanding of creative processes embedded in cultural, social, and material contexts

sublevels.name: Educational Leadership
sublevels.description: Educational Leadership covers the management, governance, and strategic direction of educational institutions and systems, focusing on leadership theory, policy, and practice at all levels of education.

data.name: Technology and Engineering
data.description: Engineering is the design and construction of systems and structures for influencing the world around us and enhancing our experience within it.
